categories.name: Find stories & patterns in sparce information

biases.name: Confabulation
biases.definition: Inventing explanations for one's actions or memories when the true cause is unknown.

positive.text: Explaining a purchase as logical when it was impulsive.
Giving a reason for forgetting something that isn't the real reason.
A witness adding details they believe are likely to be true.
A patient filling memory gaps with plausible stories.
A child inventing a reason for drawing something.

A man with Korsakoff syndrome confidently told hospital staff he had spent the morning running errands and meeting with colleagues, despite having been confined to a ward for two weeks. (Kessels et al., 2008)

After a brain operation severed the connection between his two hemispheres, a patient's verbal left hemisphere invented a perfectly plausible explanation for an action his right hemisphere had performed without the left side's awareness. (Pinto et al., 2017)

In an experiment where the face a participant had chosen as more attractive was secretly swapped for the one they had rejected, most participants did not notice and gave detailed, confident reasons for "preferring" the face they had never actually selected. (Johansson, Hall, Sikström & Olsson, 2005)

A patient recovering from a burst brain aneurysm spontaneously described meetings attended and errands completed that day, with no awareness that these events were fabrications and no memory of the injury. (Gilboa et al., 2006)

An older woman with Alzheimer's disease told her daughter she had just returned from having lunch with a friend who had in fact been dead for twelve years, describing the restaurant and conversation in detail. (El Haj & Larøi, 2017)

Research found that patients with alcoholic Korsakoff syndrome confabulated most heavily about their own personal past — producing accounts of outings, conversations, and meals that had simply never occurred. (Schnider et al., 1996)

A patient with frontotemporal dementia insisted he was currently married to a movie star and had attended a party with her the previous weekend — a detailed fabrication he believed fully and maintained even when family corrected him. (Mendez, Fras, Kremen & Tsai, 2011)

When shoppers in a supermarket were asked to sample two jams and the one they chose was secretly swapped for the other, most failed to notice and gave specific reasons for preferring the flavor they had not actually chosen. (Johansson, Hall, Sikström & Olsson, 2005)

A person waking up after surgery described in vivid detail a conversation with the surgeon that they believed had taken place during recovery, even though they had been under anesthesia throughout. (Francis et al., 2018)

A patient with severe amnesia asked what he had eaten for breakfast described a full and specific meal with no hesitation or awareness that he had no actual memory of it, and offered a completely different answer when asked again an hour later. (Schnider et al., 1996)

A brain-injured patient described attending his daughter's school recital the previous Thursday when records showed the event had taken place three years before his injury, with temporal framing of the memory shifted by years. (Johnson, O'Connor & Cantor, 1997)

Researchers found that patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex spontaneously reported visiting friends, attending events, and completing tasks on days when documentation clearly showed they had remained in inpatient care. (Gilboa et al., 2006)

Studies of Alzheimer's patients found that confabulation affected not just incidental details but core autobiographical memories — patients would describe entire chapters of their lives, including marriages and careers, that had not occurred. (El Haj & Larøi, 2017)

Patients with certain types of amnesia who were asked questions they could not possibly know the answer to would generate a confident response rather than saying "I don't know," producing elaborate, coherent, and entirely false accounts. (Moscovitch & Melo, 1997)

A study using forced confabulation found that when participants were pressured to guess answers to questions they had no knowledge of, they later misremembered their guesses as confident beliefs they had always held. (Riesthuis, Otgaar, Bogaard & Mangiulli, 2023)

In research on Korsakoff syndrome, patients not only produced false memories but also acted on them — for example, repeatedly trying to leave the ward based on plans they believed they had made, even as staff corrected them. (Arts, Walvoort & Kessels, 2017)

A healthy person confidently tells a story about a shared road trip with their college roommate that never actually happened — they have merged details from multiple real memories into a single plausible but false narrative. (Bernecker, 2017)

When a participant in a choice blindness experiment was asked to explain why they had picked a certain political position they actually opposed, most went along and gave genuine reasons for the position they had never chosen. (Johansson, Hall, Sikström & Olsson, 2005)

A study of patients with schizophrenia found that some produced confabulation-like responses when asked to explain their own behavior, offering explanations that were entirely inconsistent with what they had actually said or done. (Nahum et al., 2012)

Research on forms of confabulation found that some patients produced what are called "fantastic confabulations" — spontaneously and sincerely describing events that were physically impossible, such as living in two cities at the same time. (Nahum et al., 2012)

negative.text: Accurately recalling the true reason for a decision.
Admitting uncertainty about why something was done.
Checking notes to avoid making up explanations.

A patient with severe amnesia from hippocampal damage, when asked what she had done the previous day, simply said "I'm sorry, I really don't remember" rather than filling in the gap with a fabricated account. (Moscovitch & Melo, 1997)

Researchers found that amnesic patients without additional frontal lobe damage showed profound memory loss but did not spontaneously produce false memories to compensate — they acknowledged the gap rather than filling it in. (Moscovitch & Melo, 1997)

In the choice blindness paradigm, approximately one in four participants correctly noticed when their chosen item was swapped for the one they had rejected and pointed out the discrepancy to the experimenter. (Johansson, Hall, Sikström & Olsson, 2005)

An eyewitness to an accident told police "I only saw the car for a second, so I honestly can't tell you the color" — correctly signaling uncertainty and declining to produce a confident but potentially fabricated detail. (Mitchell & Johnson, 2009)

Healthy adults with intact frontal lobe function showed strong source monitoring ability in laboratory tasks — correctly remembering not just what they had learned, but whether they had seen it, heard it, or imagined it. (Mitchell & Johnson, 2009)

Participants in a study who were explicitly told to say "I don't know" rather than guess produced significantly fewer false memories and far less confabulatory responding than those who were pressured to always give an answer. (Riesthuis, Otgaar, Bogaard & Mangiulli, 2023)

A person asked to describe the plot of a novel she read six months ago said "I remember the general idea but I might be mixing it up with another book — I wouldn't trust my memory on the details," correctly flagging the unreliability of her recall. (Bernecker, 2017)

After a targeted neuropsychological rehabilitation program for confabulation, a brain-injured patient who previously described elaborate false events began responding to memory questions by saying "I'm not sure, I don't think I can recall that accurately." (Trivino et al., 2017)

Research comparing confabulating and non-confabulating amnesic patients of equal memory severity found that those without frontal involvement were more likely to flag uncertainty, while the confabulating group expressed high confidence in false accounts. (Johnson, O'Connor & Cantor, 1997)

Studies found that confabulation in Korsakoff syndrome often diminished as the condition became chronic even when the underlying amnesia remained severe, suggesting the brain can stop generating false memories even as the memory deficit persists. (Arts, Walvoort & Kessels, 2017)

A research participant who clearly remembered choosing the brunette in a photo comparison immediately called out the switch when handed a photo of a blonde instead, demonstrating intact introspective access to her own choice. (Johansson, Hall, Sikström & Olsson, 2005)

In a study of patients with frontal lobe damage using strategic memory retrieval tasks, those who received coaching on self-monitoring strategies began noticing and correcting their own memory errors rather than producing false reports. (Gilboa et al., 2006)

A healthy adult discussing a shared childhood memory with a sibling paused mid-story and said "Actually, wait — I think I might have heard that from mom, not from being there myself," correctly identifying the source of a potentially confused memory. (Mitchell & Johnson, 2009)

A person asked to remember what she wore to a party last month correctly acknowledged the memory as weak and vague, rather than constructing a detailed but inaccurate account with the confidence of actual recollection. (Bernecker, 2017)

In a study of patients recovering from anterior communicating artery aneurysms, a subgroup who did not have associated frontal damage showed no tendency toward spontaneous confabulation even when their episodic memory was severely impaired. (Schnider et al., 1996)

After therapy using structured reality orientation, patients who had previously confabulated daily about their location, the date, and recent events showed significant improvement and began accurately acknowledging their uncertainty rather than inventing details. (Trivino et al., 2017)

A patient with mild memory impairment asked what she'd had for breakfast that morning answered truthfully — "I think it was toast, but I'm not completely certain" — rather than generating a false memory to cover the gap. (Francis et al., 2018)

Healthy younger adults in source monitoring experiments almost never confused imagined events with experienced ones, correctly distinguishing between memories of things they had actually done versus things they had only thought about doing. (Mitchell & Johnson, 2009)

In research on the forced confabulation effect, participants who were given time to carefully reflect before answering — rather than being pressured for an immediate response — showed much lower rates of false memory formation from their initial guesses. (Riesthuis, Otgaar, Bogaard & Mangiulli, 2023)

A grandfather who could not recall whether a family story came from his own experience or from a photo album he had looked through many times said "I honestly can't tell anymore whether I really remember that or just think I do because of the pictures," demonstrating appropriate epistemic caution. (Bernecker, 2017)

biases.name: Clustering illusion
biases.definition: Seeing patterns in random data.

positive.text: Seeing patterns in lottery numbers.
Believing stock charts show hidden shapes.
Thinking coin flips with streaks are meaningful.
Seeing patterns in random noise.
Assuming disease cases cluster for a reason.

Basketball players, coaches, and fans all reported strongly believing in "hot hand" shooting streaks, but analysis of actual game records showed that a player's chance of making the next shot was statistically unaffected by whether the previous shots went in. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

During WWII, Londoners developed specific theories about which neighborhoods the German V-2 rockets were targeting and which seemed to be spared, when statistical analysis showed the impact sites were distributed entirely at random. (Clarke, 1946)

A gambler who hits the jackpot three times in a row on a slot machine concludes the machine is "hot" and plays longer, not realizing that each spin is statistically independent and the string of wins was simply a random cluster. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

When people were asked to generate a sequence that "looked random," they produced far fewer streaks of the same outcome than a truly random process would create, because they expected randomness to alternate more evenly. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

A community notices that five neighbors on the same street were diagnosed with the same rare illness and immediately suspects an environmental cause, when public health statistics show that such geographic clusters arise routinely from random chance alone. (Gilovich, 1991)

After seeing five consecutive red outcomes on a roulette wheel, a casino player becomes convinced that a streak has begun and places a large bet on red, treating an independent random event as if it carries momentum. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

Survey respondents overwhelmingly believed a basketball player was more likely to make his next shot after a string of makes than after a string of misses, even though the statistical data showed the conditional probabilities were virtually identical. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

Participants shown a truly random sequence of coin flip results (HHTHHTHHT) rated it as "non-random" and patterned, while a sequence that had been designed to avoid any runs (HTHTHTHTHT) was rated as more convincingly random. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

A sports commentator declares that a soccer striker "can't miss right now" after four consecutive goals and attributes the streak to psychological momentum, when the player's true scoring probability has not meaningfully shifted. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

An investor sees a mutual fund that outperformed the market for five straight years and attributes this to the manager's exceptional skill, not recognizing that this length of streak is statistically expected to occur in some funds purely by chance. (Gilovich, 1991)

A teacher notices that three of the top five students this year are from the same elementary school and assumes something exceptional is happening there, when three-out-of-five clustering of this type is exactly what random assignment of talent would produce. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

A poker player who wins four hands in a row starts believing he has "figured out the table" and increases his stakes dramatically, interpreting a random winning cluster as evidence of genuine skill or insight. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

Military planners looking at a map of random scatter patterns in bomb debris developed theories about enemy targeting strategy, when the distribution was simply what random dispersion looks like at the scale they were examining. (Clarke, 1946)

A manager concludes that a new workplace training program is working because the last three employees who completed it all hit their targets, without recognizing that a cluster of three successes is easily produced by chance from a random distribution. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

When shown random dot patterns projected on a screen, most participants spontaneously identified clusters of dots as meaningful constellations or shapes, even after being told the dots had been placed using a random number generator. (Gilovich, 1991)

A baseball fan tracks a pitcher's recent outings and declares him to be in a "cold streak" after four poor performances, believing his form has fundamentally changed, when the data is consistent with normal random variation around his true ability level. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

An analyst identifies what appears to be a seasonal sales pattern in three years of data and presents it as a reliable business insight, not recognizing that three years is too small a sample for genuine seasonal effects to be distinguished from random fluctuation. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

Researchers themselves fell victim to the clustering illusion in study design — planning experiments with far too few participants because small samples "looked" representative to them, leading to widespread false positives in the published literature. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A parent notices her child has scored in the top percentile on three school assignments in a row and concludes a permanent shift in ability has occurred, when this run is exactly the kind of temporary random cluster that small samples routinely produce. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

Casinos post recent roulette outcomes on a screen for players to see, knowing that this display encourages players to see streaks and patterns in random data and bet accordingly, even though no outcome influences the next spin. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

negative.text: Recognizing randomness without inferring patterns.
Using statistical tests to confirm patterns.
Accepting that streaks can occur by chance.

R.D. Clarke's statistical analysis of the WWII V-2 bomb impact sites showed that the distribution fit a Poisson process almost perfectly, meaning a trained analyst using formal methods correctly identified as random the very pattern that laypeople saw as deliberately targeted. (Clarke, 1946)

A trained epidemiologist investigating a reported cancer cluster in a suburb computed the expected random rate for a town of that size and correctly concluded the cluster was within normal statistical variation, declining to recommend an expensive environmental investigation. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

When participants were given explicit instruction about the law of large numbers and how random processes naturally produce streaks, they became significantly less likely to label genuinely random sequences as patterned. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

A statistician reviewing a chart of daily sales figures correctly concluded after running a runs test that the apparent upward trend in the last two weeks was well within what would be expected from random week-to-week variation. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

Re-analysis of the original basketball shooting data using corrected statistical methods found evidence of a small genuine "hot hand" effect in certain contexts, meaning the perceived clustering in those specific cases reflected a real phenomenon rather than an illusion. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

A quality assurance engineer using a statistical process control chart correctly determined that a run of six defective units was within normal random variation and paused the line only when the data genuinely exceeded control limits. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

A scientist who had studied probability explicitly calculated the binomial probability of five heads in a row from a fair coin as one-in-thirty-two — not unusual at all in a long sequence — and did not conclude the coin was biased. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

When researchers were shown simulated patient outcome data and explicitly told it was randomly generated before being asked to evaluate it, they were less likely to generate causal explanations for apparent clusters than when no such instruction was given. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

A basketball analyst who had received formal statistical training correctly warned a coaching staff that the player's shooting "cold streak" was likely random variation and advised against benching him based on a sample of five games. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

An investor who had studied behavioral finance recognized that a fund's five-year outperformance streak was not uncommon in a large universe of funds, correctly attributing it to chance rather than manager skill without additional evidence. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

A factory supervisor who had been trained in statistical process control recognized that three consecutive product failures were within expected random variation and correctly did not halt production or blame operators. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

An epidemiologist presented with a map of illness cases in a city correctly noted that the apparent geographic clustering was consistent with Poisson-distributed random occurrence and submitted a report recommending no further environmental investigation. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

A coach who had studied sports analytics correctly identified that a pitcher's three-game "hot streak" fell within his normal statistical range and made no adjustments to the rotation, understanding that small runs of games are unreliable indicators of true form change. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

A teacher who noticed three top students came from the same neighborhood said "that's an interesting coincidence, but five students tells us almost nothing — I'd need to see this pattern hold across many more years before drawing any conclusions." (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A person who knew basic probability correctly recognized that getting four tails in a row from a fair coin was not unusual and had no predictive bearing on the next flip, declining to change their betting behavior. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

Research participants who were given feedback after each trial about the true probability of outcomes gradually reduced their tendency to see patterns in random sequences compared to participants who received no feedback. (Gilovich, Vallone & Tversky, 1985)

A data scientist reviewing website conversion rates used a sequential testing protocol and correctly determined that the apparent spike in conversions over the past three days did not meet significance thresholds and was likely random noise. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

An actuary correctly identified that the apparent cluster of car accidents at one intersection over a two-month period was within expected random fluctuation and recommended a full-year data collection before considering any road redesign. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

When participants in a laboratory study were given large samples of data — hundreds of outcomes rather than dozens — they were significantly better at correctly recognizing random distributions as random rather than seeing illusory patterns. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A pharmacist correctly noted that three patients reporting the same side effect in one week did not represent a safety signal, explaining that the expected random rate of reports meant this kind of cluster would occur routinely by chance across all pharmacies in the region. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1972)

biases.name: Insensitivity to sample size
biases.definition: Ignoring how small samples produce unreliable results.

positive.text: Trusting a small poll as much as a large one.
Judging a restaurant from two reviews.
Drawing conclusions from a tiny medical trial.
Believing early startup success predicts long-term success.
Thinking a few lucky wins show gambling skill.

When participants were told that one hospital delivers about 45 babies a day and another delivers about 15, and asked which was more likely to record a day when over 60% of births were boys, most said both hospitals were equally likely — ignoring that small samples produce far more extreme results. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

In a study of professional psychologists, 84 researchers made decisions about study design that reflected the same bias — expecting small samples to produce results as representative and stable as large ones, leading to massively underpowered studies. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

Participants asked to estimate the probability of a group of 10 men having an average height above 6 feet gave essentially the same probability as participants asked about a group of 1,000 men, when in fact extreme averages are far more likely in small samples. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A person who asks three friends for restaurant recommendations and hears two raves and one complaint concludes confidently that the restaurant is good, treating a sample of three as if it were as reliable as a large review base. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

When counties in the U.S. with the lowest rates of kidney cancer were analyzed, they turned out to be small, rural, sparsely populated counties — the same type of counties that also had the highest rates, an apparent paradox explained entirely by the higher variability of small sample sizes. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A manager evaluates a new hiring process based on the performance of four employees and concludes it is working brilliantly, without realizing that a sample of four is far too small to distinguish a genuine effect from random variation. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

Studies showed that even researchers trained in statistics frequently planned experiments with insufficient sample sizes, because their intuition led them to overestimate how representative small samples would be of the broader population. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A journalist reports that a small town in the Midwest has the highest rate of a rare disease in the country and speculates about environmental causes, not realizing that with only a few hundred residents even one extra case dramatically inflates the rate. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A student tries a new study strategy for three tests, sees an improvement, and declares the strategy definitively superior, treating three data points as conclusive evidence of a general effect. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A person hears that a school with only 50 students had the highest math scores in the district and concludes the school must use an exceptional curriculum, when in fact small schools are mathematically expected to appear at both the top and bottom of rankings simply because of their smaller size. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

Medical students shown information about diagnostic test accuracy were found to believe that a positive result from a single test was highly conclusive, failing to consider how base rates and sample variability affect the meaning of small numbers of test results. (Hoffrage & Gigerenzer, 1998)

When people observe that 4 out of 5 of their neighbors support a local candidate, they often extrapolate this to the broader community with high confidence, without recognizing that five neighbors is far too small a sample to generalize from. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A startup announces that 80% of beta testers loved their product, not mentioning that only ten people participated in the beta — and consumers who hear this treat it as a meaningful endorsement equivalent to a large-scale survey. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

Research showed that psychologists reviewing grant proposals consistently failed to adjust their confidence in proposed findings for the sample sizes proposed, expecting clean results from groups of 20 that only large groups could reliably produce. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A coach concludes after two games that a new offensive strategy is working, not accounting for the fact that two-game samples produce extremely noisy performance data that could easily reflect random variation rather than strategy effects. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

Parents looking at school quality rankings do not realize that small schools are dramatically over-represented at the top of performance charts simply because small samples produce more extreme scores, and choose schools accordingly. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A person who reads that a supplement reduced symptoms in 7 out of 10 users in a study assumes it is highly effective, treating a sample of ten as if it were a robust clinical trial. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

When survey participants were asked to predict whether a small sample drawn from a population would mirror the population's demographics closely, most said yes — underestimating the large random swings that can occur in small draws. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A journalist covering election polling confidently declared a race over when a poll of 200 people showed one candidate 12 points ahead, not adjusting for the much larger margin of error that comes with a smaller sample. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

Research consistently shows that people expect a short sequence of coin flips — say, five flips — to reflect the 50/50 probability of the overall population, when in fact extreme splits like five heads in a row are common in short sequences and carry no special meaning. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

negative.text: Preferring large, representative samples.
Rejecting conclusions drawn from tiny datasets.
Asking for more data before deciding.

A clinical researcher correctly computed the statistical power needed to detect a clinically meaningful effect and determined she needed 400 participants, not 40, before the trial could produce trustworthy conclusions. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A pollster reported election results with an explicit margin of error tied to the sample size, correctly communicating to readers that a poll of 500 people carries a larger uncertainty range than a poll of 5,000. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A physician told a patient that a single positive screening result was not enough to confirm a diagnosis, explaining that false positives occur often enough in rare conditions that a follow-up test on a larger confirmatory sample was needed. (Hoffrage & Gigerenzer, 1998)

A researcher reviewing a colleague's study noted that the effect was interesting but declined to draw firm conclusions, correctly pointing out that a sample of 18 participants was far too small to distinguish a genuine effect from random noise. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A consumer reading about a supplement that "9 out of 10 users found effective" looked up that only 10 people were tested and correctly discounted the claim, recognizing that the sample was far too small to be informative. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

An epidemiologist investigating disease rates in small rural counties explicitly noted in her report that small population sizes would produce extreme rates by chance and declined to recommend targeted intervention without confirming the pattern in larger datasets. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A statistician advising a school district correctly explained that small schools appear disproportionately at the top of achievement rankings not because of better instruction but because small samples generate extreme scores more often, and recommended averaging over multiple years. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A person who had taken a statistics course recognized that her survey of 12 friends about a new app told her very little about general user experience, and refrained from recommending it to the company as evidence of broad appeal. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A fund manager who correctly understood sampling variability declined to attribute a three-year streak of outperformance to skill, noting that in a large universe of funds, streaks of this length arise from chance alone at meaningful rates. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A journalist covering a story about a town with a high rate of a rare illness correctly led her article by noting the town had only 2,000 residents, explaining that a single extra case in a small population dramatically inflates rates. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A teacher who had studied educational research recognized that a pilot program showing improvement in one class of 25 students was promising but not conclusive, and advocated for a full-school trial before adopting the program district-wide. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A coach reviewing two weeks of data from a new training routine correctly identified that this was too short and too small a sample to attribute changes in performance to the program rather than to normal within-season variation. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

When given training that explicitly showed how extreme outcomes are more probable in smaller samples through interactive simulation, participants in a study significantly improved their ability to correctly identify which hospital was more likely to produce unusual outcomes. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A market researcher correctly explained to a client that focus group data from 8 participants could identify themes and hypotheses but could not be generalized to the broader population the way a survey of 500+ people could. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A person looking at the performance of two investment portfolios over six months recognized that six months was too short a window to draw meaningful conclusions and chose to wait for at least three years of data before evaluating manager skill. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A policy analyst reviewing a pilot program in two cities correctly stated in her report that outcomes in such small samples could not be considered representative of what would happen if the policy were rolled out nationally. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A scientist reviewing a study that found a striking drug effect in 15 patients correctly insisted on replication with a much larger sample before including the finding in a review paper, recognizing that small samples frequently produce results that do not hold up. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A student who had just learned about sampling variability in class correctly told her study group that the results from their informal class survey of 20 people should not be presented as representative of the university's whole student body. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

An HR professional proposing a new interview process correctly insisted on tracking outcomes across at least 200 hires before drawing conclusions, recognizing that the first 10 hires would reflect too much random variability to assess the process fairly. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1971)

A participant in the original hospital problem experiment who answered correctly — identifying the smaller hospital as more likely to record extreme outcomes — explained that smaller groups produce more variable results, demonstrating explicit awareness of the relationship between sample size and statistical reliability. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

biases.name: Neglect of probability
biases.definition: Ignoring actual likelihoods when judging risk.

positive.text: Fearing flying more than driving.
Buying warranties for low-risk items.
Overreacting to rare dramatic news.
Ignoring odds when choosing lottery numbers.
Assuming a risky investment is safe because it feels right.
A person refuses to fly after hearing about a plane crash on the news, even though car travel is statistically far more dangerous per mile traveled. (Slovic, Fischhoff & Lichtenstein, 1982)

After winning a small prize in the lottery once, a teenager buys a ticket every week convinced that winning again is essentially guaranteed, ignoring that the odds remain astronomically small. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)

Parents refuse to vaccinate their child because they heard of a child who had a severe reaction, treating the extremely rare adverse event as if it were a near-certainty. (Fischhoff & Beyth-Marom, 1983)
A gambler keeps placing bets on red at roulette because black has come up five times in a row, treating the next spin as though red is now essentially certain to appear. (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974)

A homeowner refuses to purchase earthquake insurance despite living in a high-risk zone because no quake has occurred in their lifetime, treating a low-frequency catastrophic risk as negligible. (Kunreuther et al., 1978)

A manager dismisses the need for cybersecurity protocols because the company has never been hacked before, ignoring actuarial data showing small businesses face significant breach risk. (Anderson et al., 2019)
A student skips studying for a test because they have never failed before, treating the low but real probability of failure as zero. (Kahneman, 2011)
A politician votes against pandemic preparedness funding because no major outbreak has hit the country in decades, treating the low annual probability as equivalent to impossibility. (Sunstein, 2002)

Research participants in a classic study rated the probability of dying from a vivid rare cause (shark attack) as higher than dying from common causes like heart disease, reversing actual probabilities. (Lichtenstein et al., 1978)

A new driver assumes they will never be in an accident because they feel confident behind the wheel, ignoring that roughly 1 in 100 drivers will be involved in an injury crash each year. (Svenson, 1981)

A smoker dismisses warnings about lung cancer risk because they know an 80-year-old who has smoked all their life, treating the relative rarity of surviving heavy smoking as proof the risk is negligible. (Weinstein, 1989)

Participants in a study were willing to pay the same amount to remove one contaminant from a lake whether the stated risk was 1-in-10,000 or 1-in-100,000, showing insensitivity to actual probability magnitudes. (Baron & Greene, 1996)

After a neighborhood burglary, residents who previously ignored alarms installed expensive security systems, overweighting the now-salient risk far beyond what crime statistics justified. (Viscusi & Zeckhauser, 2006)

A startup founder insists their product will definitely succeed because they personally know two founders who struck it rich, ignoring the base-rate failure rate of over 90% for new ventures. (Camerer & Lovallo, 1999)
Investors poured money into lottery-like penny stocks that offered tiny chances of enormous gains while ignoring higher-probability moderate returns from index funds. (Kumar, 2009)

A patient who had a one-in-a-million adverse drug reaction refuses all future medications in that class, treating recurrence as virtually certain despite negligible base rates. (Chapman & Elstein, 2000)

A town that experienced a rare hundred-year flood twice in a decade built no new flood barriers because officials believed another major flood in the near term was essentially impossible. (Kunreuther & Pauly, 2004)

In a classic experiment, subjects paid nearly as much to reduce a small risk from 5% to 0% (eliminating it entirely) as to reduce a large risk from 50% to 5%, showing pseudocertainty preferences that ignore probability magnitudes. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979)

A jury awarded enormous punitive damages to a plaintiff who suffered a rare but dramatic injury even though expert testimony showed the defendant's product was safer than alternatives, because the vivid harm overshadowed probability reasoning. (Sunstein et al., 2002)

An investor pulled all funds out of the stock market after a single day's large drop, treating a low-probability catastrophic loss as imminent rather than weighing long-run statistical returns. (Benartzi & Thaler, 1995)

negative.text: Comparing risks using actual statistics.
Choosing insurance based on expected value.
Evaluating investments using probability models.

An actuary calculates the expected payout for a life insurance portfolio by carefully weighting each cause-of-death probability against its frequency in the covered population before setting premiums. (Promislow, 2011)
A public health official uses age-stratified COVID-19 hospitalization rates to prioritize vaccine rollout to the elderly first, correctly weighting the much higher risk in that group. (CDC, 2021)
A structural engineer applies established safety factors based on load probability distributions rather than ignoring low-frequency extreme load scenarios when designing a bridge. (ASCE, 2016)

A doctor correctly explains to a patient that a screening test has a 0.1% false-positive rate and walks through Bayes' theorem to interpret a positive result accurately before recommending further testing. (Gigerenzer et al., 1995)

After reviewing crime statistics showing that their neighborhood's burglary rate has actually fallen by 60% over five years, a homeowner decides not to upgrade their security system further. (Bureau of Justice Statistics, 2019)

A financial advisor uses Monte Carlo simulations with accurate return distributions to show a client the realistic range of retirement outcomes rather than treating any single scenario as certain. (Leibowitz & Henriksson, 1988)
A meteorologist explains that the 5% chance of rain tomorrow means the forecast model gives genuinely low but non-zero probability to precipitation, not that rain is impossible. (Murphy, 1993)

A judge instructs jurors to weigh the statistical rarity of a DNA match against the possibility of lab error, asking them to reason from actual probability estimates before reaching a verdict. (Koehler, 1993)

A safety officer at a chemical plant uses fault-tree analysis with actual failure probabilities for each component to calculate overall system risk, rather than ignoring low-frequency events. (Vesely et al., 1981)

A consumer chooses comprehensive car insurance after calculating the expected value of the coverage given their regional accident rates and repair costs, correctly accounting for probability in the decision. (Phelps, 2012)
A chess player who loses a game analyzes the specific move where they made a strategic error rather than concluding that all future games are unwinnable. (Charness, 1981)
A company's risk committee assigns quantitative probability estimates to each identified risk and ranks them by expected loss before allocating mitigation resources. (ISO 31000, 2018)

An epidemiologist concludes a drug reduces heart attack risk by 30% after running a properly powered randomized trial with preregistered statistical thresholds, reflecting true causal probability. (Hennekens & Buring, 1987)
A pilot uses published engine-failure probability data and checklists to weigh when a precautionary landing is warranted rather than dismissing the risk as too unlikely to plan for. (FAA, 2016)
A voter reads polling data showing a candidate with a 78% win probability and understands this means the opposing candidate still has a meaningful 22% chance of winning. (Silver, 2012)

A health economist correctly applies disability-adjusted life year calculations that weight each health outcome by both its probability and severity rather than treating rare severe outcomes as negligible. (Murray & Lopez, 1996)
A flood insurance underwriter sets premiums using 100-year floodplain maps and actuarial tables that correctly reflect annual exceedance probabilities rather than ignoring the base rate. (FEMA, 2020)

A researcher computes the positive predictive value of a biomarker correctly using Bayes' theorem, accounting for the low prevalence of the disease before reporting clinical utility. (Altman & Bland, 1994)

A teenager learns that the lifetime risk of being struck by lightning is approximately 1 in 15,000 and decides not to change their outdoor behavior significantly while still avoiding open fields during storms. (NOAA, 2022)

A procurement officer selects a supplier after reviewing their historical delivery-failure rate of 2% rather than dismissing or overweighting this risk without calculating its expected impact on operations. (Zsidisin, 2003)

biases.name: Anecdotal fallacy
biases.definition: Using personal stories as if they prove general rules.

positive.text: Claiming a diet works because one friend lost weight.
Saying a city is unsafe due to one bad experience.
Believing a medicine works because a relative improved.
Rejecting vaccines due to one negative story.
Judging a school from one student's experience.
A smoker dismisses lung cancer statistics by saying his grandfather smoked two packs a day and lived to 95, using this single case as evidence that smoking is safe. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)

A parent refuses to vaccinate their child because they personally know one child who developed a fever after a vaccine, ignoring large-scale safety data showing vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. (Kata, 2012)
A person argues that seatbelts are dangerous by pointing to a news story they heard about someone who survived a crash because they were not buckled in. (Evans, 1986)
A politician dismisses poverty statistics by citing their own rags-to-riches story as proof that anyone can succeed if they just work hard enough. (Nisbett & Borgida, 1975)
A manager rejects a new hiring policy after one bad experience with a candidate it produced, ignoring the policy's strong overall track record across hundreds of hires. (Nisbett et al., 1983)
Someone argues that a neighborhood is safe because they walked through it once without incident, disregarding the area's documented crime statistics. (Slovic et al., 1979)
A person insists that a homeopathic remedy works because it cured their own cold, not considering that colds resolve on their own and the remedy may have had no effect. (Ernst, 2002)

Research participants updated their beliefs about a racial group far more strongly after hearing one vivid personal story about a member than after receiving equivalent statistical data about the group. (Nisbett & Borgida, 1975)
A traveler warns others that an entire country is dangerous after being pick-pocketed once during a two-week trip, dismissing overall safety statistics for that destination. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)
An employer refuses to hire from a particular university after one poor hire from there, despite strong aggregate performance data from hundreds of graduates at that school. (Nisbett et al., 1983)

A diet blogger cites her own 30-pound weight loss on a specific plan as proof the diet works for everyone, without acknowledging that research shows mixed and often unsustained results. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)
Someone argues against wearing helmets while cycling because they know a person who was injured more seriously because their helmet came off during an accident. (Thompson et al., 1989)
A jury member dismisses statistical evidence about wrongful convictions because they have never personally known anyone who was wrongfully convicted. (Nisbett & Borgida, 1975)

A student argues that a particular study method is ineffective because it did not work for their roommate, overriding a large body of cognitive research supporting that method. (Dunlosky et al., 2013)
An investor ignores diversification advice after hearing about a friend who got rich by putting all their money into one stock. (Gilovich, 1991)

A person concludes that therapy is useless because their cousin tried it and said it did not help, overriding meta-analyses showing therapy is effective for a broad range of conditions. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)
A landlord refuses to rent to pet owners after one tenant's dog damaged the property, treating that single experience as representative of all pet owners. (Nisbett et al., 1983)

A parent dismisses gender-gap research in STEM by pointing to their daughter who excelled in math, treating one case as a refutation of a documented population-level pattern. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)
A user review claiming a product completely transformed someone's life influences purchasing decisions more than a peer-reviewed study showing no significant benefit. (Nisbett & Borgida, 1975)
Someone argues that drunk driving laws are unnecessary by describing a relative who drove home drunk for 30 years without ever causing an accident. (Evans, 1986)

negative.text: Relying on large-scale evidence instead of anecdotes.
Recognizing that one case doesn't prove a trend.
Asking for controlled studies before concluding.

A physician tells a patient that while their neighbor recovered quickly from the treatment, the clinical trial data show only a 40% response rate, so the neighbor's story should not drive their decision. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)

A public health official presents population-level vaccination safety data and explicitly notes that individual stories of adverse events, while real, do not reflect the statistical risk for most people. (Kata, 2012)
A researcher discounts their own informal observation about a drug and designs a randomized controlled trial to test whether the pattern holds at the population level. (Ernst, 2002)
A financial advisor explains to a client that hearing about one person who got rich in cryptocurrency does not change the statistical risk profile of the investment. (Gilovich, 1991)

Participants given both statistical data and an anecdote about welfare spending weighted the statistical data significantly more heavily when they were explicitly instructed to assess evidence quality. (Nisbett & Borgida, 1975)
A policymaker requests a representative community survey rather than basing legislation on the three constituent stories they received in their inbox. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)
A sports analyst uses a player's multi-season performance averages and advanced metrics rather than highlighting one memorable game when evaluating the player's true ability. (Gilovich, 1991)

A hiring committee that tracks long-term employee outcomes uses aggregate data from multiple cohorts to evaluate the success of their hiring process rather than remembering one outstanding or one disappointing hire. (Nisbett et al., 1983)
A jury is instructed by the judge to base their verdict on the evidence presented in court, and they explicitly set aside personal anecdotes they know about similar cases. (Nisbett & Borgida, 1975)

A traveler consults crime rate statistics, State Department advisories, and reviews from multiple sources before deciding whether to visit a destination, rather than relying on one friend's bad experience. (Slovic et al., 1979)
A parent deciding on a school compares standardized test scores, teacher turnover rates, and class sizes rather than relying on what a neighbor said about the school. (Nisbett et al., 1983)

A science journalist explicitly notes in their article that the compelling patient story they opened with is not representative of the average outcome based on clinical trial data. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)
A medical journal editor rejects a case report as sufficient evidence for a new treatment and requests data from a properly controlled study. (Ernst, 2002)

A student who hears an inspiring story about a college dropout who became a billionaire correctly identifies the outcome as an exceptional outlier rather than a representative result. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)

An organization evaluating a wellness program compares outcomes across all enrolled employees using pre- and post-measures rather than collecting only testimonials from satisfied participants. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)

A voter evaluates a candidate's economic policy by examining unemployment and GDP data from their tenure rather than accepting the candidate's own account of one business they helped save. (Gilovich, 1991)

A product reviewer tells readers that their personal experience with a product was unusually positive and directs them to aggregate rating distributions for a more accurate picture. (Nisbett & Borgida, 1975)

A nutritionist explains to a client that knowing one person who lost weight on a particular diet is not sufficient evidence that the diet works and points them toward systematic reviews of the research. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)
A cyclist decision to wear a helmet is based on population-level injury data rather than a single story about someone whose helmet failed. (Thompson et al., 1989)

A therapy skeptic reads a meta-analysis of hundreds of randomized controlled trials and revises their view rather than continuing to rely on their cousin's negative personal experience. (Lilienfeld et al., 2010)

biases.name: Illusion of validity
biases.definition: Overestimating accuracy of judgments despite weak evidence.

positive.text: A recruiter trusting gut feelings.
A trader believing their predictions are reliable.
A teacher thinking they always spot cheating.
A coach believing first impressions predict success.
A manager trusting personality tests too much.

Army officers felt highly confident in their predictions about which recruits would succeed as officers even though follow-up studies showed their accuracy was close to chance. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)

A stock analyst feels certain that a company will outperform the market based on a pattern of consistent quarterly growth, even though research shows most analysts cannot beat index fund returns. (Kahneman, 2003)

A hiring manager feels very confident about a candidate who gave a smooth and coherent interview, even though research consistently shows that unstructured interview performance is a poor predictor of job success. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)
A weather forecaster assigns 90% confidence to a prediction that historically has been correct only about 70% of the time. (Lichtenstein et al., 1982)
A clinical psychologist was highly confident in diagnoses drawn from consistent MMPI profiles even in cases where the profiles had been constructed from random data. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)
A wine sommelier confidently names the vintage year of a wine based on taste, even though blind-tasting studies show expert accuracy is only marginally above chance. (Kahneman, 2003)
A police officer is certain a suspect is lying based on body language cues, even though research shows body language is a poor indicator of deception. (Kahneman, 2003)
A teacher feels sure a student will struggle all year in math after seeing two early poor assignments, even though early performance is a weak predictor of long-term outcomes. (Kahneman, 2003)
A coach is convinced they can spot athletic talent in a single tryout, even though their track record of identifying future stars is no better than chance. (Gilovich, 1991)
Experienced radiologists felt highly confident in time-pressured diagnoses even when their accuracy was no better than that of more cautious readers. (Lichtenstein et al., 1982)
Investors felt very confident that a company with three great quarters would keep outperforming, even though regression to the mean makes this unlikely. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)
Real estate appraisers reported high confidence in their valuations even though two independent appraisers of the same property frequently differed by 10% or more. (Kahneman et al., 2021)

A school admissions officer feels certain that an applicant's personal essay is a strong predictor of college success, even though research shows essays have minimal predictive power. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)
Sentencing judges expressed high confidence in their decisions even though two judges reviewing identical cases frequently imposed very different sentences. (Kahneman et al., 2021)
A long-time poker player is convinced they can reliably read other players, even though variance in card outcomes frequently overwhelms any true skill in reading tells. (Kahneman, 2003)

A therapist who identifies consistent themes across a client's stories becomes highly confident in a diagnosis, even though those themes are consistent with multiple different diagnostic categories. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)

A financial adviser believes their pattern-reading of stock charts gives them a reliable edge in the market, despite evidence that technical analysis does not reliably outperform random selection. (Kahneman, 2003)
Doctors overestimated the diagnostic accuracy of a physical examination technique even after being told the objective accuracy rate for that test. (Lichtenstein et al., 1982)

A personality test clinician felt confident that consistent test results revealed a client's true nature, even when those same scales have been shown to have limited real-world predictive validity. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)

An experienced chef feels certain a new recipe will be a hit before testing it with diners, relying on culinary intuition even though expert taste predictions frequently diverge from consumer response. (Kahneman, 2003)

negative.text: Revising judgments when evidence contradicts intuition.
Using validated metrics instead of gut feelings.
Acknowledging uncertainty in predictions.

A forecasting researcher runs calibration checks and finds that meteorologists' confidence ratings closely match their actual long-run accuracy rates, showing valid confidence. (Lichtenstein et al., 1982)

An admissions office that tracks four-year student outcomes adjusts its confidence in interview evaluations downward after seeing that interview scores have weak correlations with GPA. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)

A physician explicitly states they are 60% confident in a preliminary diagnosis and orders confirmatory tests before acting, calibrating their expressed certainty to the actual state of evidence. (Lichtenstein et al., 1982)
An investment firm adopts algorithmic stock selection after data consistently show that human analysts' confident picks do not outperform the algorithm over a ten-year period. (Kahneman, 2003)

A hiring committee switches from unstructured interviews to structured, scored assessments after reviewing research showing that unstructured interviews have low predictive validity. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)
A clinical psychologist uses validated actuarial risk tools rather than clinical intuition alone after comparing the accuracy of both approaches in their practice. (Kahneman, 2003)
A sports scout requests three full seasons of performance data before finalizing talent assessments, having learned that early impressions frequently do not hold up. (Gilovich, 1991)
A poker player who tracks their results over hundreds of sessions correctly identifies that their win streaks reflect variance rather than reliable skill in reading opponents. (Kahneman, 2003)

A radiologist who participates in a peer review audit discovers their false positive rate is higher than expected and lowers their confidence threshold for borderline cases. (Lichtenstein et al., 1982)

A weather service that publishes calibration data shows that its probability forecasts closely track actual outcomes over thousands of forecasts, demonstrating genuine predictive validity. (Lichtenstein et al., 1982)

An HR department that benchmarks hiring prediction accuracy concludes that personality test scores do not warrant high confidence and supplements them with work-sample tests. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)
A financial analyst correctly applies historical base rate returns rather than trusting their intuitive read of a company's leadership team when making a recommendation. (Kahneman, 2003)
A teacher assigns grades based on multiple assessments spread across the semester rather than relying on confident impressions formed during the first week of class. (Kahneman, 2003)
A judge who learns about the noise in judicial sentencing explicitly requests a structured checklist to reduce unjustified confidence variation across similar cases. (Kahneman et al., 2021)
A policy analyst refuses to make confident 10-year projections about a regulation's impact, citing the poor track record of long-range forecasting in their domain. (Lichtenstein et al., 1982)
A pilot trained in crew resource management double-checks instruments before trusting their confident intuitive sense of the aircraft's position. (Lichtenstein et al., 1982)
A researcher designs a study to test whether their clinical intuition is predictively valid before incorporating it into treatment decisions. (Kahneman & Tversky, 1973)
A master sommelier correctly acknowledges in a blind tasting study that their accuracy in identifying vintage years is only modest, consistent with the objective data. (Kahneman, 2003)

An experienced appraiser who participates in a calibration exercise is surprised to find that their estimates vary significantly across two independent appraisals of the same property and adjusts their confidence accordingly. (Kahneman et al., 2021)
A football coach who has access to years of data on fourth-down conversion rates uses those rates to make decisions rather than relying on a confident gut sense of when to go for it. (Gilovich, 1991)

biases.name: Masked man fallacy
biases.definition: Assuming two descriptions differ because one detail differs.

positive.text: Thinking Clark Kent and Superman are different.
Rejecting that a masked performer is a known celebrity.
Believing a suspect isn't the same person due to disguise.
Assuming two photos differ due to filter or time of day.
Thinking someone in costume is a different person.

negative.text: Recognizing someone despite changes in appearance.
Using contextual clues to confirm identity.
Checking evidence before concluding two people differ.

biases.name: Regency illusion
biases.definition: Overweighting recent events over earlier ones.

positive.text: Judging a student by recent grades only.
Assuming a stock is strong due to recent gains.
Thinking a friend's recent behavior defines them.
Judging a restaurant by the last visit only.
Believing a team is great after a short streak.

negative.text: Evaluating performance over long-term trends.
Considering full history instead of recent events.
Avoiding snap judgments based on short-term changes.

biases.name: Gambler's fallacy
biases.definition: Believing past random events influence future ones.

positive.text: Expecting tails after many heads.
Thinking roulette is due for black.
Believing a losing streak must end soon.
Assuming a slot machine will pay out soon.
Thinking future exam questions might be similar.

negative.text: Recognizing each event is independent.
Using probability theory to judge randomness.
Accepting that streaks don't change future odds.

biases.name: Hot-hand fallacy
biases.definition: Believing success streaks will continue.

positive.text: Thinking a basketball player will keep scoring.
Believing a trader on a streak will keep winning.
Assuming a student will keep answering correctly.
Thinking a gamer on a streak is unbeatable.
Expecting a salesperson to keep closing deals.

negative.text: Evaluating performance using long-term averages.
Recognizing streaks can be random.
Checking actual skill metrics instead of streaks.

biases.name: Illusory correlation
biases.definition: Perceiving relationships between unrelated variables.

positive.text: Believing full moons cause strange behavior.
Thinking certain clothes predict personality.
Linking unrelated events as cause and effect.
Assuming two random trends are connected.
Believing lucky charms influence outcomes.

negative.text: Testing correlations statistically.
Rejecting associations without evidence.
Recognizing coincidences as random.

biases.name: Pareidolia
biases.definition: Seeing meaningful images in random stimuli.

positive.text: Seeing faces in clouds.
Seeing animals in rock formations.
Seeing shapes in tree bark.
Seeing figures in shadows.
Seeing patterns in static.

negative.text: Identifying objects only when evidence is clear.
Recognizing random shapes as meaningless.
Using instruments instead of intuition to interpret images.

biases.name: Anthropomorphism
biases.definition: Attributing human traits to non-human entities.

positive.text: Talking to a pet as if it understands language.
Naming a car and treating it like a person.
Assuming a robot has emotions.
Thinking weather is intentional.
Believing a plant is 'happy' or 'sad.'

negative.text: Recognizing machines lack emotions.
Understanding animal behavior scientifically.
Avoiding human-like interpretations of natural events.

categories.name: Traits from stereotypes, generalities, & histories

biases.name: Group attribution error
biases.definition: Assuming an individual's traits reflect their group, or a group's decisions reflect each member.

positive.text: Believing a coworker is organized because their team is known for efficiency.
Assuming a student is athletic because their school excels in sports.
Thinking a neighbor is wealthy because their neighborhood is upscale.
Believing a club member shares all the club's values.
Assuming a colleague is introverted because their department is quiet.

negative.text: Evaluating a coworker solely on their individual performance.
Asking a student about their own interests instead of assuming them.
Recognizing that people in the same group can have very different views.

biases.name: Ultimate attribution error
biases.definition: Explaining out-group failures as internal flaws and in-group failures as external circumstances.

positive.text: Excusing your team's loss as bad luck but blaming the rival team's loss on incompetence.
Assuming your group's mistake was due to pressure but another group's mistake was due to laziness.
Believing your political group acted under constraints but the other acted maliciously.
Explaining your culture's problems as situational but others' as inherent.
Seeing your friend's failure as circumstantial but a stranger's as personal.

negative.text: Acknowledging that both groups face similar external pressures.
Judging individuals from another group by their specific context.
Admitting your own group can be at fault internally too.

biases.name: Stereotyping
biases.definition: Assigning traits to individuals based solely on group membership.

positive.text: Assuming a programmer likes video games.
Believing artists are emotional.
Thinking tall people play basketball.
Assuming older adults dislike technology.
Believing scientists are introverted.

negative.text: Asking someone about their interests instead of assuming them.
Recognizing that group labels don't predict personality.
Hiring based on skills and evidence rather than group traits.

biases.name: Essentialism
biases.definition: Believing groups have inherent, unchangeable characteristics.

positive.text: Thinking creativity is something people are born with.
Believing certain cultures are naturally better at math.
Assuming personality traits are fixed from birth.
Thinking gender determines career ability.
Believing intelligence is predetermined.

negative.text: Accepting that people can change over time.
Recognizing the role of environment and learning.
Encouraging growth through practice and feedback.

biases.name: Functional fixedness
biases.definition: Seeing objects only in terms of their traditional uses.

positive.text: Using a mug only for drinking instead of as a pen holder.
Not realizing a shoe can hammer a nail.
Failing to use a scarf as a makeshift rope.
Ignoring that a phone flashlight can light a room.
Not thinking to use a book as a doorstop.

negative.text: Using a paperclip to pick a lock in an emergency.
Turning a box into a temporary table.
Using a scarf as a bag strap when one breaks.

biases.name: Moral credential effect
biases.definition: Feeling licensed to act less morally after doing something moral.

positive.text: Donating once and then feeling justified in ignoring future charity.
Helping a friend and then being rude to a stranger.
Recycling and then wasting energy later.
Volunteering once and then judging others harshly.
Making one ethical choice and then indulging in selfish behavior.

negative.text: Continuing to act kindly after doing a good deed.
Reflecting on past good actions as motivation to do more good.
Avoiding using past morality as an excuse for bad behavior.

biases.name: Just-world hypothesis
biases.definition: Believing people get what they deserve, leading to victim-blaming.

positive.text: Assuming a successful person must have worked hard.
Believing good things happen to good people.
Thinking misfortune reflects personal flaws.
Assuming kindness guarantees good outcomes.
Believing effort always leads to success.

negative.text: Recognizing that bad things can happen to good people.
Acknowledging the role of luck and systemic factors.
Supporting victims without blaming them for their situation.

biases.name: Argument from fallacy
biases.definition: Assuming that if an argument contains a fallacy, its conclusion must be false.

positive.text: Rejecting a claim because someone argued it poorly.
Dismissing a point due to a flawed analogy.
Ignoring evidence because one example was weak.
Rejecting a conclusion because a speaker misspoke.
Assuming a belief is wrong because someone defended it badly.

negative.text: Separating the quality of reasoning from the truth of the conclusion.
Re-examining a claim using better evidence.
Accepting that a poorly argued claim can still be true.

biases.name: Automation bias
biases.definition: Overtrusting automated systems and ignoring contradictory human judgment.

positive.text: Trusting GPS directions even when the road is closed.
Accepting spellcheck suggestions without reviewing.
Believing a medical device's reading without question.
Letting software choose the best photo automatically.
Relying on autopilot settings without checking.

negative.text: Double-checking GPS directions against road signs.
Questioning a suspicious medical reading with a manual check.
Overriding an automated system when it clearly malfunctions.

biases.name: Bandwagon effect
biases.definition: Adopting beliefs or behaviors because many others do.

positive.text: Buying a product because it's trending.
Supporting a sports team because everyone else does.
Joining a social media challenge.
Following a fashion trend without preference.
Agreeing with a popular opinion to fit in.

negative.text: Choosing a product after independent research despite its unpopularity.
Supporting an unpopular but well-reasoned position.
Refusing to join a trend that doesn't match your values.

biases.name: Placebo effect
biases.definition: Experiencing real changes due to belief in a treatment rather than the treatment itself.

positive.text: Feeling pain relief after taking a sugar pill.
Sleeping better after drinking 'relaxation tea' with no active ingredients.
Improving mood after a fake vitamin.
Believing a workout supplement boosts energy when it doesn't.
Feeling calmer after a 'stress patch' with no chemicals.

negative.text: Experiencing no change after taking an inert pill you don't believe in.
Improving only after receiving an active, evidence-based treatment.
Showing symptoms that don't respond to fake treatments but do respond to real ones.

categories.name: More fond of what we are familiar with

biases.name: Halo effect
biases.definition: Letting one positive trait influence overall judgment of a person.

positive.text: Assuming someone is smart because they are attractive.
Thinking a friendly coworker is also highly competent.
Believing a well-dressed applicant is more qualified.
Rating a student higher because they participate often.
Trusting a charismatic speaker more than the evidence warrants.

negative.text: Evaluating someone based on detailed performance metrics.
Separating appearance from ability when judging.
Recognizing strengths and weaknesses independently.

biases.name: In-group bias
biases.definition: Favoring people from one's own group.

positive.text: Choosing a teammate from your own club.
Trusting advice from someone who shares your background.
Supporting a coworker because they're from your department.
Giving more patience to someone from your community.
Assuming your group's ideas are better.

negative.text: Judging individuals based on merit rather than group membership.
Giving equal consideration to out-group members.
Seeking diverse perspectives intentionally.

biases.name: Not invented here
biases.definition: Rejecting ideas because they come from outside one's group.

positive.text: Dismissing a tool because another company created it.
Ignoring research from another department.
Rejecting a solution because it wasn't developed internally.
Preferring a worse internal method over a better external one.
Avoiding collaboration with outside experts.

negative.text: Evaluating ideas based on quality, not origin.
Adopting an external solution after testing it.
Collaborating openly with outside contributors.

biases.name: Cross-race effect
biases.definition: Difficulty recognizing faces of races different from one's own.

positive.text: Confusing two unfamiliar faces from another race.
Struggling to recall a person met briefly from another race.
Believing two out-group individuals look similar.
Failing to identify an out-group person in a lineup.
Recognizing familiar individuals from any race equally well.

negative.text: Using objective identifiers instead of relying on memory.
Improving recognition through repeated exposure.
Acknowledging uncertainty instead of making assumptions.

biases.name: Cheerleader effect
biases.definition: People appear more attractive in groups than individually.

positive.text: Thinking a group photo looks better than solo shots.
Perceiving a group of friends as more appealing together.
Finding a sports team photo more attractive than individuals.
Believing a group of coworkers looks more polished.
Rating a band photo as more attractive than solo portraits.

negative.text: Judging attractiveness based on individual photos.
Evaluating people one at a time without group influence.
Noticing that group context doesn't change your perception.

biases.name: Well-traveled road effect
biases.definition: Underestimating travel time on familiar routes and overestimating unfamiliar ones.

positive.text: Thinking your usual commute is shorter than it is.
Assuming a new route will take much longer.
Believing a familiar path is always faster.
Choosing the same route because it feels quicker.
Estimating unfamiliar travel times conservatively.

negative.text: Using GPS estimates instead of intuition.
Timing routes to compare objectively.
Become well-prepared before go to an unfamiliar place.

biases.name: Out-group homogeneity bias
biases.definition: Seeing out-group members as more similar than they really are.

positive.text: Believing all members of another culture think alike.
Assuming a rival team's fans share identical traits.
Thinking another department's employees all behave the same.
Believing an out-group has uniform preferences.
Assuming individuals from another group vary widely.

negative.text: Asking questions to learn individual differences.
Recognizing diversity within all groups.
Avoiding generalizations about out-groups.

biases.name: Reactive devaluation
biases.definition: Devaluing proposals simply because they come from an opposing group.

positive.text: Rejecting a good idea because a rival suggested it.
Assuming a negotiation offer is bad due to its source.
Dismissing a policy because it came from another party.
Undervaluing a suggestion from a competing team.
Rejecting a compromise because of who proposed it.

negative.text: Evaluating proposals based on content, not origin.
Accepting good ideas regardless of source.
Separating personal feelings from objective assessment.

biases.name: Positivity effect
biases.definition: Older adults tending to focus more on positive than negative information.

positive.text: Remembering pleasant events more than unpleasant ones.
Paying more attention to uplifting news.
Choosing to spend time with positive people.
Recalling positive traits of others more easily.
Focusing on optimistic interpretations.

negative.text: Remembering negative and positive events equally.
Evaluating information without emotional filtering.
Giving equal weight to neutral, positive, and negative cues.

categories.name: Simplify numbers

biases.name: Mental accounting
biases.definition: Treating money differently depending on arbitrary categories.

positive.text: Saving a tax refund while overspending from a paycheck.
Refusing to spend gift money on necessities.
Splurging with 'vacation money' but being frugal at home.
Treating casino winnings as disposable.
Separating budgets for groceries and entertainment rigidly.

negative.text: Viewing all money as interchangeable.
Making decisions based on total financial picture.
Combining funds instead of labeling them emotionally.

biases.name: Normalcy bias
biases.definition: Underestimating the possibility or impact of disasters.
