biases.name: Post-purchase rationalization
biases.definition: a specific form of hindsight/choice bias: you remember your choice more positively and alternatives more negatively.

positive.text: After voting, you think your candidate was 'obviously best.'
After picking a partner, you see others as less compatible.
After choosing a project topic, others seem boring.
After picking a route, other routes 'would've been worse.'
After selecting a phone, other brands seem inferior.

negative.text: You acknowledge uncertainty at the time.
You compare using evidence, not loyalty.
You avoid rewriting history to feel consistent.
You keep notes of why you chose it.
You stay open to revising future choices.

biases.name: Choice-supportive bias
biases.definition: noticing and interpreting information in ways that match your expectations (what you 'look for' is what you 'see').

positive.text: Expect rudeness — you notice neutral comments as rude.
Think you're bad at math — notice mistakes more than successes.
Believe a class is boring — notice every dull moment.
Assume a place is unsafe — focus on suspicious cues.
Expect a friend to ignore you — interpret late replies as rejection.

negative.text: You consider multiple interpretations.
You ask for clarification instead of assuming.
You gather more data over time.
You use objective measures (rubrics, logs).
You check your assumption with the person.

biases.name: Selective perception
biases.definition: a researcher/observer's expectations influence what they notice and record.

positive.text: Teacher expects a student to do poorly — grades harsher.
Coach expects laziness — notices only low effort.
Doctor expects anxiety — overlooks physical causes.
Judge expects arrogance — interprets confidence as disrespect.
Researcher expects effect — records ambiguous data as positive.

negative.text: Blind/double-blind procedures.
Pre-registered criteria for scoring.
Multiple independent raters.
Use standardized rubrics.
Actively look for disconfirming observations.

biases.name: Observer expectancy effect
biases.definition: a type of expectancy bias where the experimenter unintentionally influences participants/outcomes.

positive.text: Giving subtle hints to 'correct' answers.
Different tone/body language changes participant responses.
Leading questions in an interview study.
Smiling more when the 'right' behavior appears.
Recording borderline results as success.

negative.text: Double-blind design.
Scripted instructions only.
Automated measurements.
Separate data collection from analysis.
Independent replication.

biases.name: Experimenter's bias
biases.definition: people change behavior because they know they're being observed or measured.

positive.text: Work faster when the teacher walks by.
Eat healthier during a diet study.
Drive more carefully with a dashcam.
Perform better when being graded live.
Act 'nicer' when a parent watches.

negative.text: Unobtrusive measures (anonymous, passive).
Long-term observation so it fades.
Hidden/neutral observation when ethical.
Compare to baseline behavior logs.
You behave the same even when watched.

biases.name: Observer effect
biases.definition: general tendency: expectations shape perception, interpretation, and memory.

positive.text: Expect an exam to be hard — anxiety makes it feel harder.
Expect a movie to be bad — you notice flaws.
Expect pain from a shot — it hurts more.
Expect someone to be mean — you see sarcasm in neutral words.
Expect a stock to rise — you interpret news as bullish.

negative.text: You hold expectations lightly and test them.
You gather evidence before concluding.
You consider alternative explanations.
You separate feelings from facts.
You update expectations when data changes.

biases.name: Expectation bias
biases.definition: avoiding information you find unpleasant, even if it's important.

positive.text: Not checking bank balance to avoid stress.
Ignoring a bad grade email.
Avoiding health test results.
Not reading feedback on your work.
Refusing to look at market losses.

negative.text: You face the data early to act.
You schedule check-ins (finance/grades/health).
You get support to process bad news.
You turn info into an action plan.
You prefer knowing over avoiding.

biases.name: Ostrich effect
biases.definition: believing a statement is true because it feels personally meaningful ('it fits me').

positive.text: Horoscopes feel accurate to you.
Personality tests seem 'spot on' without evidence.
You accept vague 'predictions' as true.
You think a quote is about you specifically.
You see patterns/messages in random events.

negative.text: You look for specific, testable claims.
You compare to base rates ('Would fit anyone?').
You ask for evidence beyond feelings.
You test predictions over time.
You accept uncertainty when evidence is weak.

biases.name: Subjective validation
biases.definition: misinformation continues to influence thinking even after correction.

positive.text: You remember the rumor, not the correction.
A retracted news story still shapes your opinion.
'It was debunked' but it still 'feels' true.
You repeat the false claim accidentally later.
First explanation sticks even after update.

negative.text: You replace it with a clear alternative explanation.
You repeat the correction more than the myth.
You avoid restating the myth unnecessarily.
You cite reliable sources when correcting.
You update your mental model explicitly.

biases.name: Continued influence effect
biases.definition: rejecting new ideas automatically because they challenge established beliefs/practices.

positive.text: Dismissing handwashing because 'we've never done that.'
Rejecting a new method without testing.
Calling new evidence 'nonsense' instantly.
Refusing to change study habits despite proof.
Rejecting innovation because it feels threatening.

negative.text: You test new ideas with small trials.
You ask 'What evidence supports/contradicts this?'
You separate identity from beliefs.
You update when results show improvement.
You stay curious rather than defensive.

biases.name: Semmelweis reflex
biases.definition: rejecting new evidence/ideas automatically because they conflict with existing beliefs or traditions.

positive.text: Doctors dismiss handwashing evidence because 'we've never needed it.'
A teacher rejects a new grading method without trying it.
Someone refuses climate data because it clashes with their worldview.
A company ignores a better workflow because it's 'not how we do things.'
You reject a study tip just because it's different from your habit.

negative.text: You test the new idea in a small trial first.
You ask 'What evidence supports this?' before rejecting it.
You separate 'unfamiliar' from 'wrong.'
You update beliefs when results consistently improve outcomes.
You stay curious and compare alternatives using the same standard.

categories.name: Flaw in others more easy to see than in ourselves

biases.name: Bias blind spot
biases.definition: seeing biases in others but not in yourself; thinking you're more objective than other people.

positive.text: You say 'everyone else is biased' but assume your view is just facts.
You spot confirmation bias in a friend but not when you do it.
You think ads manipulate others, not you.
You judge others' mistakes as 'irrational,' yours as 'reasonable.'
You believe you're less influenced by social media than classmates.

negative.text: You catch yourself saying 'I'm being objective,' then you pause and ask, 'What would change my mind?'
You invite a friend to critique your argument and you actually revise it after their feedback.
You run the same decision through a checklist (pros/cons, base rates, alternatives) even when you feel 'sure.'
You notice you're harsher on others' mistakes than your own, and you correct for it ('same standard').
You keep a 'times I was wrong' note and use it to spot patterns in your thinking.

biases.name: Naïve cynicism
biases.definition: assuming other people's actions are driven by selfish motives (cynical explanations), even when kinder explanations fit.

positive.text: Someone compliments you — 'they want something.'
A friend helps you — 'they're trying to look good.'
A teacher gives advice — 'they're controlling.'
A classmate shares notes — 'they're fishing for info.'
A charity post — 'just for clout.'

negative.text: Someone compliments your work and you accept it at face value instead of assuming they want something.
A classmate offers help and you take it as genuine support, not manipulation.
You interpret a late reply as 'they're busy,' not 'they're ignoring me on purpose.'
You see a charity fundraiser and check transparency/evidence rather than assuming it's a scam.
You assume most people mean what they say unless there's clear evidence otherwise.

biases.name: Naïve realism
biases.definition: believing you see the world objectively, and people who disagree are uninformed/irrational/biased.

positive.text: 'If they disagree, they didn't read the facts.'
You think your political view is just common sense.
Group argument: you assume you're the only logical one.
You treat your opinions as reality, not perspective.
You're shocked others interpret the same event differently.

negative.text: You say 'This is how I see it,' instead of 'This is how it is,' and you ask how others interpret it.
Two people watch the same event and disagree; you treat both views as plausible, not 'one must be lying.'
You separate facts from interpretations ('He didn't reply' vs 'He doesn't care').
You notice your mood changes your judgment and you wait before making a final call.
You update your belief after new evidence, even if your first impression felt 'obviously true.'

categories.name: Edit and reinforce memories after the fact

biases.name: Spacing effect
biases.definition: Spaced practice improves long-term memory more than cramming.

positive.text: Studying weekly remembers more than one-night cramming.
Reviewing vocabulary over days improves recall.
Practicing piano daily beats one long session.
Revisiting notes weekly strengthens retention.
Spaced quizzes improve exam performance.
Bahrick et al. (1993): 13 spaced sessions (56-day gaps) matched 26 massed sessions for 9-year vocabulary retention.
Rohrer & Taylor (2006): College students' 4-week math test scores nearly doubled with distributed vs. massed practice.
Taylor & Rohrer (2008): Spaced geometry practice produced 78% vs. 38% on delayed tests.
Sobel et al. (2011): One-week spacing outperformed massed learning in real fifth-grade classrooms.
Cumulative final exams force spaced learning and boost long-term retention.

negative.text: Cramming helps short-term recall before test.
One session suffices for simple facts.
Repetition without gaps still works briefly.
Single intensive workshop teaches basic skills.
Immediate practice boosts temporary performance.
Massed practice (cramming) outperforms spacing when tests are taken immediately after the study session.
Wiseheart et al. (2017): No spacing effect found in piano learning for a 17-note sequence or song accuracy across different lag intervals.
Some preschool-age children don't show spacing benefits, though recent research suggests they may still benefit.
Spacing fails with paraphrased repetitions (changed surface structure) and under lengthy lag conditions.
One classroom study found no benefit of spacing for children in grades 2-6, though the "massed" condition may have been spread across multiple days.

biases.name: Suggestibility
biases.definition: Memories change due to leading questions or suggestions.

positive.text: After being asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed,' witnesses later remember broken glass that never existed.
A child repeatedly asked, 'Did the man touch you?' eventually recalls being touched, despite no such event occurring.
An officer hints 'we caught the guy,' leading a witness to confidently identify an innocent person.
Parents tell a story about you getting lost as a toddler; years later, you vividly 'remember' it — though it never happened.
A therapist suggests childhood trauma, and over time the client forms detailed memories aligned with that suggestion.

When people are asked how fast cars were going when they "smashed" into each other rather than "hit," they later remember seeing broken glass at the scene that was never there. (Loftus & Palmer, 1974)

After being told repeatedly that a classroom visitor named Sam Stone was clumsy and careless, many preschoolers later reported watching him rip a book and dirty a teddy bear, even though he never touched either. (Leichtman & Ceci, 1995)

When family members told participants they had gotten lost in a shopping mall as a young child, roughly a quarter of them later formed detailed memories of an event that their relatives confirmed never happened. (Loftus & Pickrell, 1995)

When surrounded by a room full of people who all give the same obviously wrong answer, about 37% of people go along with the group and say the same wrong thing even when they can see with their own eyes that it is incorrect. (Asch, 1951)

When an officer tells a witness after a lineup "you identified the right person," the witness later recalls having been far more certain and having had a much clearer view during the crime, even when they picked the wrong person. (Douglass & Steblay, 2006)

Patients who were told a sugar pill was a powerful painkiller reported genuinely feeling less pain, and brain scans showed real changes in the parts of the brain that process pain. (Colloca & Barsky, 2020)

When people were told that the wine they were drinking cost $45 instead of $5, they rated its taste as significantly more enjoyable, and brain scans confirmed that the pleasure centers of their brains were actually more active. (Plassmann et al., 2008)

When some clients sought therapy for mental health struggles and therapists suggested their problems might stem from repressed childhood abuse, some clients subsequently developed detailed memories of abuse that had never occurred. (Otgaar et al., 2019)

When teachers were told that certain randomly selected students were about to experience an intellectual growth spurt, those students showed significantly greater IQ gains by the end of the year than their peers. (Rosenthal & Jacobson, 1968)

Adolescents who regularly see friends and influencers on social media promoting certain eating habits or body ideals are more likely to adopt those same behaviors and perceptions about their own bodies. (Chung et al., 2021)

When students in one school reported strange symptoms like dizziness and nausea after believing they had been exposed to a toxic smell, the illness rapidly spread to dozens of other students even after investigators found no harmful substance in the building. (Bartholomew & Wessely, 2002)

When a doctor grimaces and says "this is going to hurt" before a routine injection, patients report significantly more pain than when the same procedure is described neutrally, because the suggestion shapes what they expect to feel. (Colloca et al., 2019)

Young children who are asked the same question repeatedly during an interview tend to change their answer on subsequent asks, interpreting the repeated question as a signal that their first answer was wrong. (Ceci & Bruck, 1995)

When suspects are subjected to long, pressured interrogations where investigators repeatedly hint they could not possibly have committed the crime, some innocent people eventually come to doubt their own memories and believe they may actually be guilty. (Gudjonsson, 2021)

A person who reads online that a supplement causes headaches is significantly more likely to report headaches after taking it than someone who was not given that information beforehand, even when the pill contains no active ingredient. (Häuser et al., 2012)

When people overhear a friend confidently misremember a detail about a shared event, they often update their own memory of the event to match the friend's version, even when their original memory was accurate. (Zaragoza et al., 2007)

People who score higher on tests of imaginative suggestibility are more likely to respond to nonhypnotic suggestions and to produce vivid mental experiences simply because someone tells them to imagine something in a certain way. (Braffman & Kirsch, 1999)

Younger children are substantially more susceptible to accepting false suggestions from an authority figure than older children or adults, meaning age is one of the strongest predictors of how easily someone's memory can be shaped by an outside source. (Ceci & Bruck, 1995)

When a friend insists you loved a movie you actually felt lukewarm about, you may walk away genuinely remembering you enjoyed it, because social suggestion can quietly reshape even recent subjective experiences. (Loftus, 2005)

negative.text: Neutral questions preserve original memories.
Independent recall resists suggestion.
Recording events reduces later distortion.
Multiple sources confirm consistent memories.
Careful interviewing avoids leading questions.

When eyewitnesses are told before an interview that the information they are about to hear may not be reliable, they are significantly less likely to incorporate that misleading information into their memory of the original event. (Chan et al., 2020)

When just one person in a group gives the correct answer instead of going along with the wrong majority, conformity rates drop by as much as 80%, showing that a single ally can almost entirely cancel out group pressure to accept a false suggestion. (Asch, 1956)

When engineering students in the UK were put through the same line-judgment task that produced 37% conformity in American students in the 1950s, only one out of 396 trials showed conformity, demonstrating that domain expertise and cultural context can block suggestibility almost entirely. (Perrin & Spencer, 1981)

People with higher working memory capacity are consistently better at recognizing and rejecting misleading post-event information, meaning cognitive resources serve as a natural buffer against suggestibility. (Greene et al., 2020)

Even people with extraordinarily detailed autobiographical memories, who can recall daily events from decades ago, are just as susceptible to suggestion and false memory formation as people with ordinary memory, showing that memory strength alone does not protect against suggestibility. (Patihis et al., 2013)

When participants pay close attention to an event and encode it with high visual salience, younger adults are significantly less likely to form false memories in response to misleading information about that event. (Fraisse et al., 2024)

When a witness is told that the person who provided them with post-event information was untrustworthy or incompetent, the misinformation effect is substantially reduced, showing that perceived source credibility determines whether a suggestion takes hold. (Dodd & Bradshaw, 1980; Zaragoza et al., 2007)

When people are taught about how human memory works and how easily it can be distorted, they show measurably lower rates of accepting false suggestions in subsequent eyewitness memory tests. (Szpitalak & Polczyk, 2019)

When a doctor describes a procedure using neutral or positive framing instead of leading with warnings about pain, patients report experiencing significantly less discomfort, showing that the nocebo effect depends on specific communication choices and can be avoided. (Colloca et al., 2019)

A person who witnesses a car accident and tells no one about it before being questioned is much less likely to incorporate misleading details into their account than someone who discussed it with others first, because retelling creates new opportunities for suggestion to enter memory. (Zaragoza et al., 2007)

When older adults are asked about contradictory misinformation that directly conflicts with something they already know, they are actually less likely to accept it than younger adults, showing that life experience with a topic can resist certain types of suggestion. (Huff & Umanath, 2018)

A person who holds a strong prior belief, backed by personal experience, in a political or factual matter tends not to update that belief in response to casual social suggestion, because motivated reasoning acts as a shield against external influence. (Ecker et al., 2022)

When someone openly knows they are taking a sugar pill with no active ingredients, the placebo effect still occurs for symptoms like pain and fatigue, but it does not change biological markers like cholesterol, meaning suggestion only influences things the brain can modulate. (Kaptchuk et al., 2010)

When younger adults strongly encode the details of a witnessed event, they show little to no difference in false memory rates compared to older adults, meaning encoding strength can override age-related suggestibility differences. (Wylie et al., 2002)

When people actively think about where information came from rather than just what it says, they are less likely to confuse a suggested detail with something they actually witnessed, because source monitoring acts as a mental check against suggestibility. (Lindsay & Johnson, 1989)

Suggestibility toward nocebo effects is a trait that varies significantly between individuals, meaning a warning about side effects that triggers real symptoms in one person may have no effect at all on another person who scores low on suggestibility measures. (Colloca & Barsky, 2020)

When a child is interviewed using open-ended, non-leading questions that do not imply a preferred answer, they are far more likely to report only what they actually remember, showing that the absence of suggestion is what keeps testimony accurate. (Ceci & Bruck, 1995)

A mechanic who notices a car part looks wrong will not change their assessment just because a customer insists it is fine, because domain-specific expertise creates confidence in one's own judgment that resists social suggestion. (Perrin & Spencer, 1981)

When people are shown that the source of a piece of misinformation had a conflict of interest or an ulterior motive, they substantially reduce their reliance on that suggestion even without receiving a direct correction of the false information. (Ecker et al., 2024)

When eyewitnesses answer questions privately rather than in the presence of others, they show significantly lower rates of conformity to incorrect information, because social pressure requires an audience to generate the discomfort that drives suggestibility. (Asch, 1956)

biases.name: False memory
biases.definition: Remembering events that never actually happened.

positive.text: Recalling childhood event that never occurred.
Remembering meeting someone never met.
Believing you visited a place unvisited.
Recalling words not presented in lists.
Remembering imagined story as real.
Loftus (1970s): Participants exposed to misleading information about a car accident reported seeing broken glass and higher speeds when the question used "smashed" vs. "hit"
Loftus's "Lost in the Mall" study: 25% of participants developed false memories of being lost in a shopping mall as a child; a 2019 replication found 35%
Loftus et al. (1978): Participants shown a yield sign but told they saw a stop sign'the overlap made it easier to accept misinformation
Loftus & colleagues: Misleading information can actually overwrite the original memory of an event, especially with increasing age
Misinformation effect research: Participants generally endorse misinformation quickly and with high confidence, qualifying as genuine false memory

After studying a list of words all related to sleep, like "bed," "rest," and "dream," people confidently report having seen the word "sleep" on the list even though it was never there. (Roediger & McDermott, 1995)

When college students were told a false story about spilling punch at a wedding as a child and asked about it across multiple interviews, about 25% eventually developed detailed memories of an event that never happened. (Hyman et al., 1995)

When family members told participants they had been lost in a shopping mall as a child, roughly a quarter of them formed vivid memories of an event their relatives confirmed never occurred. (Loftus & Pickrell, 1995)

When people were shown a digitally altered photo of themselves as a child in a hot air balloon, about half of them developed detailed personal memories of a ride that never took place. (Wade et al., 2002)

When participants asked to imagine a minor childhood event in detail, like accidentally breaking a window, their confidence that the event had really happened increased significantly compared to events they had not imagined. (Garry et al., 1996)

After being told as part of a study that they had gotten sick from eating strawberry ice cream as a child, up to 40% of participants came to believe this false memory and later said they did not want to eat that food. (Bernstein et al., 2005)

When people were interviewed multiple times using suggestive techniques about a crime they had never committed, around 70% developed detailed false memories of committing assault or theft as a teenager. (Shaw & Porter, 2015)

People who had been awake all night were significantly more likely than well-rested people to incorporate misleading post-event details into their memories of a witnessed event, showing that fatigue directly increases false memory formation. (Lo et al., 2016)

Students who wrote down their memory of hearing about the 9/11 attacks were just as likely to have inconsistent details months later as those who recorded an ordinary memory, showing that even vivid emotional memories become distorted over time. (Talarico & Rubin, 2003)

When people saw a news article about a hurricane alongside a photo of a damaged village, they falsely remembered the article mentioning more deaths and injuries than it actually described, showing that images can distort what we think we read. (Garry et al., 2007)

Participants who attended an event together and then discussed it with each other afterward often incorporated details mentioned by their companion into their own memory, even when those details were things only the other person had seen. (Meade & Roediger, 2002)

About 40% of students who were interviewed about the Challenger space shuttle disaster two and a half years after it happened gave accounts that contradicted what they had written the day after the explosion, yet rated their confidence in the later version as high. (Neisser & Harsch, 1992)

People sometimes remember turning off the stove or taking their medication because it is part of their usual routine, not because they actually have a clear memory of doing it that specific time, making routine actions especially prone to false memory. (Johnson et al., 1997)

When a witness overhears another witness describe a detail they did not see themselves, they frequently incorporate that detail into their own account and later recall it as something they personally witnessed. (Gabbert et al., 2003)

When people repeatedly imagined performing a simple action like flipping a coin, they later remembered having actually done it, showing that mental rehearsal can create false memories of actions that were only imagined. (Goff & Roediger, 1998)

A person who dreams vividly about a conversation with a friend may wake up genuinely believing the conversation happened, because the brain uses similar processes to store imagined and real experiences. (Johnson et al., 1997)

Even people with extraordinarily detailed autobiographical memories who can recall events from decades ago were just as likely as ordinary people to form false memories when shown misleading information in a study. (Patihis et al., 2013)

When people are asked misleading questions shortly after watching a film clip of a car accident, they later remember seeing things that were not in the film, like broken glass or a barn that was never there. (Loftus et al., 1978)

Children who were told four weeks before a classroom visit that a guest named Sam Stone was clumsy later reported seeing him rip a book and dirty a teddy bear during his visit, even though he had done neither. (Leichtman & Ceci, 1995)

People who read heavily covered news stories and social media posts about events they did not personally witness often later confuse things they read about with things they actually saw, blurring the line between their memory and media consumption. (Schacter, 2021)

negative.text: Verifying memories with photos and records.
Distinguishing imagination from actual experiences.
Cross-checking events with others' accounts.
Using diaries to confirm past events.
Recognizing uncertainty in vague recollections.
Loftus (2005): Some people are resistant to misinformation effects under certain conditions, though the exact boundary conditions remain unclear
False memories fail when semantic similarity is weak'changing details that have no semantic relation to the original event produces minimal false memory effects
Okado & Stark (2005): Brain scans showed some individuals' neural activity patterns predicted they would resist misinformation, maintaining accurate memories
Strong encoding of original events reduces susceptibility to false memories from later misinformation
Warnings about potential misinformation can reduce false memory formation in some studies

When people are warned before an interview that some information they are about to hear may be inaccurate, they show significantly lower rates of incorporating that false information into their memories of the original event. (Chan et al., 2020)

When someone correctly remembers that they did not take their medication this morning because they have a specific, distinctive memory of skipping it while rushing out the door, they are accurately tracking a real event rather than constructing a false one. (Johnson et al., 1997)

A skilled mechanic who correctly recalls that a car came in with a specific noise last Tuesday is demonstrating accurate memory for a distinctive and professionally relevant event, not a false memory. (Perrin & Spencer, 1981)

When someone accurately remembers the main plot of a novel they read last year but forgets minor details like character names, this is normal memory decay and forgetting rather than a false memory, because no incorrect information has been added. (Schacter, 2021)

When participants were warned before a memory test that the word lists they had studied were designed to make them think of related words that were not actually on the list, they showed significantly reduced false recognition of those lure words. (Roediger & McDermott, 1995; Gallo, 2006)

When people are shown a factual correction to something they read previously and told to stop relying on the original information, they can reduce their use of the incorrect information when forming judgments, even though the false memory influence is rarely eliminated entirely. (Ecker et al., 2010)

Implanting a false memory of receiving a painful medical procedure as a child was significantly harder than implanting a plausible false event like getting lost in a mall, showing that extremely implausible events do not easily become false memories. (Pezdek & Hodge, 1999)

A witness who correctly identifies a perpetrator in a lineup and maintains that identification consistently across multiple interviews is demonstrating a stable accurate memory, not a false memory, even though false memories can arise in similar situations. (Wells & Bradfield, 1998)

When someone recalls a strongly emotional and personally significant event, like the birth of a child, with high accuracy across many years because they have thought and talked about it frequently, this is accurate autobiographical memory maintained through rehearsal rather than a false memory. (Talarico & Rubin, 2003)

When people are asked to monitor the source of information they are recalling, for example by asking whether a detail came from the original video or a later summary, they show reduced false memory errors because source monitoring counteracts false attribution. (Lindsay & Johnson, 1989)

People with higher working memory capacity are better at rejecting misleading post-event details and keeping their original memory intact, showing that cognitive resources can prevent false memory formation under the right conditions. (Greene et al., 2020)

When a child gives a consistent, unprompted, and spontaneous account of something that happened without being asked leading questions, they are demonstrating accurate recall rather than a false memory created by external suggestion. (Ceci & Bruck, 1995)

A person who forgets where they put their keys is experiencing normal forgetting, not a false memory, because they have not formed an incorrect memory of a specific wrong location to replace the correct one. (Schacter, 2001)

When participants in a study correctly rejected a word as not being on a list they studied, even when that word was semantically related to many words that were on the list, they were successfully using distinctive memory features to resist false recognition. (Gallo, 2006)

When older adults are asked to remember events that directly contradict something they know from experience, they are actually less likely to accept those contradictory suggestions than younger adults, showing that some forms of life knowledge protect against false memory. (Huff & Umanath, 2018)

When people are trained on how memory works and taught to notice the difference between things they actually experienced and things they only heard about, they subsequently make fewer false memory errors in memory tests. (Szpitalak & Polczyk, 2019)

A trauma survivor who accurately and consistently recalls the key details of what happened to them across multiple accounts over time is demonstrating genuine memory, not a false memory, even though traumatic memories can sometimes be distorted. (Otgaar et al., 2019)

When someone accurately remembers having already told a particular joke to a friend and stops themselves from repeating it, they are exercising successful source monitoring and accurate memory retrieval rather than experiencing a false memory. (Johnson et al., 1997)

When participants in a study correctly remembered details from a video they watched even after being exposed to misleading information about those details, they were maintaining accurate memories by successfully resisting misinformation rather than forming false ones. (Chan et al., 2020)

When a person confidently and accurately recalls that a meeting was scheduled for Thursday and checks their calendar to confirm, they are using external verification to anchor their memory to reality rather than relying on reconstructive processes that could lead to error. (Johnson et al., 1997)

biases.name: Cryptomnesia
biases.definition: Forgetting source, believing recalled idea is original.

positive.text: A student repeats a clever argument in an essay, genuinely believing they invented it — it was from last week's lecture.
A songwriter creates a melody, later realizing it closely matches a song they heard months ago.
Someone tells a funny story, convinced it's theirs, but it actually came from a friend.
A designer proposes a 'new' logo concept that subconsciously copies something seen online.
A writer pitches a plot idea, unaware it mirrors a novel they once read.
Brown & Murphy (1989): In group category tasks, people inadvertently plagiarized 3-9% of the time by regenerating another person's idea as their own
George Harrison's "My Sweet Lord": Faced legal consequences for subconsciously copying the melody despite a genuine belief it was original
Helen Keller: Inadvertently borrowed from a story read to her years earlier, leading to plagiarism accusations
Nietzsche case (analyzed by Jung): Likely unconsciously integrated material encountered decades earlier from Burckhardt's work into his philosophical writing
Marsh & Bower (1994): Word-search puzzle task showed substantially higher cryptomnesia rates (3-5%) than earlier category studies, manipulated by retention interval and encoding depth

When participants in a group brainstorming task were later asked to come up with new ideas in the same category, they repeated ideas suggested by other group members between 3 and 9 percent of the time while genuinely believing those ideas were their own. (Brown & Murphy, 1989)

When people competed against a computer partner in a word-search puzzle and were later asked to find new words, they regularly produced words the computer had already found and presented them as original, showing that cryptomnesia occurs even in simple problem-solving tasks. (Marsh & Bower, 1993)

When participants were put under time pressure to generate new ideas quickly, they plagiarized significantly more of their partners' previous ideas than when they had time to think, because speeded responding prevents the source-monitoring check that stops idea theft. (Marsh et al., 1997)

George Harrison sincerely believed he composed "My Sweet Lord" from scratch, but a court found in 1976 that the melody was unconsciously copied from "He's So Fine" by the Chiffons, a song he had heard years earlier and forgotten. (Bright Tunes Music v. Harrisongs Music, 1976)

Helen Keller wrote a short story at age eleven that closely mirrored a fairy tale she had been read four years earlier and had no memory of, genuinely believing she had invented the entire story herself. (Taylor, 1965; Wikipedia on Cryptomnesia)

A person who hears a clever phrase during a conversation and uses it two weeks later in a meeting as if they thought of it on the spot is experiencing cryptomnesia, because the content of the idea outlasted the memory of where it came from. (Marsh et al., 1997)

(Brown & Murphy, 1989)

When participants were performing a distracting secondary task while generating ideas, they showed higher rates of inadvertent plagiarism, confirming that any reduction in available mental resources makes it harder to track whose idea is whose. (Macrae et al., 1999)

A writer who reads dozens of articles while researching a topic and later drafts a piece may reproduce a particularly vivid phrase or argument as if it were their own, because the content of what was read outlives memory of the specific source. (Johnson et al., 1997)

When ideas from a previous week's group session were plagiarized in a follow-up meeting, participants plagiarized approximately 20 percent of the supposedly new ideas they offered, reproducing content from the earlier session without any awareness of doing so. (Marsh & Landau, 1995)

Friedrich Nietzsche reproduced a passage almost word for word from a book he had read years earlier in a chapter of "Thus Spoke Zarathustra," and Carl Jung later identified this as a case of cryptomnesia rather than deliberate copying. (Taylor, 1965; Wikipedia on Cryptomnesia)

A student who spent the previous semester reading extensively about a topic may write a thesis chapter and unknowingly incorporate an argument from a forgotten paper, genuinely experiencing the idea as something they reasoned out independently. (Marsh et al., 1997)

When participants were induced into a happy mood before a word puzzle task, they made significantly more source errors and claimed more of their partner's answers as their own than participants who were in a sad or neutral mood. (Gingerich & Dodson, 2013)

People in a group conversation frequently pick up a word or phrasing used by someone else minutes earlier and then use it again as if they coined it themselves, a phenomenon researchers identify as a common everyday occurrence of cryptomnesia. (Marsh et al., 1997)

A society can collectively remember that civil rights improved while forgetting the specific minority groups whose activism made that change happen, which is called social cryptomnesia and represents the same source-forgetting mechanism at a cultural scale. (Butera et al., 2009)

When two sources of ideas looked and sounded more similar to each other, participants were more likely to confuse which ideas came from themselves versus a partner, showing that perceptual distinctiveness of the source protects against cryptomnesia. (Macrae et al., 1999)

A songwriter who hums a melody they believe is original may unknowingly be reconstructing a tune they heard years ago on the radio, because music is particularly vulnerable to cryptomnesia given how often melodies are absorbed passively without deliberate attention to their source. biases.name: Identifiable victim effect
biases.definition: People help specific visible individuals more than anonymous statistical victims.

positive.text: She donated instantly after seeing one injured puppy on social media.
He ignored disaster statistics but paid hospital bills for one neighbor.
Students fundraised harder after meeting a single affected classmate.
Viewers cried for one refugee child, ignoring thousands displaced.
Volunteers rallied once hearing one survivors personal story.

negative.text: You donate equally to anonymous charities.
You help based on statistics, not faces.
You support large-scale relief efforts.

biases.name: Appeal to novelty
biases.definition: Preferring new options simply because they seem fresh or innovative.

positive.text: He bought the newest phone despite perfectly working old model.
Students tried flashy apps instead of proven study methods.
Managers adopted trendy frameworks without evidence.
She ordered experimental drinks over reliable favorites.
Investors chased newest startups blindly.

negative.text: You choose an older product because it works better.
You keep proven study methods.
You reject flashy but ineffective apps.

biases.name: Hyperbolic discounting
biases.definition: Preferring immediate rewards over larger delayed benefits irrationally.

positive.text: He chose gaming tonight instead of studying for future scholarships.
She spent savings now rather than investing for retirement.
Students skipped homework for instant social media scrolling.
Speeding to save minutes even when accidents could occur
Workers cashed bonuses immediately.

negative.text: You save money instead of buying gadgets.
You study now for future success.
You delay dessert for health.

categories.name: Favor completing when  time & energy invested

biases.name: Backfire effect
biases.definition: Contradictory evidence strengthens existing beliefs instead of changing them.

positive.text: Facts about vaccines made him more resistant.
A voter is shown verified facts disproving their candidate's claim — and becomes even more loyal, calling the sources biased.Climate data hardened denial.
A skeptic sees scientific data about rising temperatures but doubles down, saying scientists exaggerate for funding.
When presented with official documents disproving a conspiracy, believers argue the documents are part of the cover-up.
A student receives evidence their answer is wrong, yet insists the teacher misunderstood and defends their original reasoning more aggressively.

negative.text: You change your opinion after seeing strong evidence.
You admit you were wrong.
You update beliefs when presented with facts.

biases.name: Endowment effect
biases.definition: Valuing owned objects more than identical unowned objects.

positive.text: He overpriced his used laptop because ownership made it feel more valuable than market alternatives.
Someone refuses to sell a mug they own for $5, despite originally paying only $2 for it.
Students demanded more money for books they owned than they would pay to borrow identical copies.
Homeowners often inflate their house's value simply because it belongs to them personally.
Collectors rejected fair trades because giving up owned items felt like a personal loss.

negative.text: She sold her old phone cheaply, valuing it no more than identical used models.
Owning the mug did not increase its value compared with store alternatives.
He judged the product solely by features, ignoring personal ownership.

biases.name: Pseudo certainty effect
biases.definition: Avoiding risk when gains seem certain, ignoring overall probabilities.

positive.text: She chose a guaranteed small prize instead of a larger option with higher expected value.
Investors avoided minor risks even when probabilities favored better long-term returns.
People choose a sure $50 discount now over a probabilistic $100 savings later, ignoring expected value.
Students preferred guaranteed grades rather than risk assessment-based evaluations with higher potential scores.
Shoppers favored guaranteed coupons over lottery-style promotions with better expected savings.

negative.text: She chose the option with higher expected value despite uncertain outcomes.
He accepted some risk after carefully comparing total probabilities.
They evaluated all possible outcomes instead of focusing on guaranteed gains.

biases.name: Unit bias
biases.definition: Preferring single units regardless of appropriate quantity.

positive.text: He ate the entire giant muffin because it was considered one serving.
She poured a full glass every time, regardless of how much she actually wanted to drink.
Students read only one article because assignments framed it as a single required unit.
Gym members finish one full plate simply because it is served as one portion.
A person eats the entire large bag of chips because it's labeled one serving, regardless of portion size.

negative.text: He adjusted portion size based on hunger rather than eating a fixed unit.
She split the package to consume an appropriate amount.
They ignored default units and measured quantities precisely.

biases.name: Disposition effect
biases.definition: Selling winning investments early, holding losing ones too long.

positive.text: He sold profitable stocks quickly to lock gains instead of letting winners grow further.
She held onto failing shares for years, hoping losses would eventually reverse.
Traders locked in gains prematurely while refusing to accept losses on declining investments.
Investors sell winning stocks quickly but hold losing stocks too long, hoping they'll recover.
Portfolios stagnated because losses were held too long and gains were cut too early.

negative.text: She held winning stocks long-term while quickly selling poor investments.
He rebalanced objectively, ignoring gains or losses.
Investment decisions were based on future prospects, not past performance.

biases.name: Zero-risk bias
biases.definition: Preferring complete elimination of small risks over reducing larger risks.

positive.text: Parents demanded zero peanut policies despite evidence showing minimal actual allergy risks.
Cities overfunded extremely rare hazards while ignoring more probable public safety threats.
Patients chose zero-risk surgeries even when slightly risky alternatives had better outcomes.
Managers eliminated tiny defects while ignoring larger systemic operational failures.
Consumers bought unnecessary insurance simply because it promised complete risk elimination.

negative.text: They preferred reducing major risks instead of eliminating minor ones completely.
She chose the option with greatest overall risk reduction.
The policy focused on proportional risk reduction rather than zeroing small threats.

biases.name: Generation effect
biases.definition: Information remembered better when self-generated.

positive.text: Students remembered answers better when they wrote them themselves during practice sessions.
She recalled self-made flashcards more effectively than information from prewritten notes.
He memorized song lyrics faster by composing his own melodies.
Teams remembered ideas better when they brainstormed them collaboratively.
Kids recalled invented stories more vividly than stories they only read.

negative.text: He remembered the definition equally well after reading it carefully.
Listening attentively produced the same recall as self-generating answers.
Provided examples were remembered without personal generation.

biases.name: Processing difficulty effect
biases.definition: Harder-to-process information feels more valuable or memorable.

positive.text: Blurred slides seemed deeper and more important simply because they required extra effort to understand.
Complex fonts made simple content feel more intelligent and authoritative to readers.
Dense articles impressed readers despite offering no additional meaningful insights.
Messy notes felt more meaningful because they demanded extra cognitive effort to interpret.
Cryptic quotes sounded profound even when their actual message was vague.

negative.text: Clear, fluent text felt more trustworthy than complex wording.
Easy-to-read instructions were judged more useful.
Simplicity increased confidence rather than reducing perceived value.

biases.name: IKEA effect
biases.definition: Valuing self-assembled products more than identical preassembled ones.

positive.text: People value a wobbly desk they assembled themselves more than a sturdier, store-bought one.
She loved a handmade shelf more than professionally manufactured alternatives.
Students favored posters they created together over professionally designed ones.
Parents cherished children's DIY crafts more than store-bought decorations.
Gamers valued custom-built characters more than default in-game options.

negative.text: She preferred the factory-assembled table over the one she built herself.
Self-assembly did not increase his valuation of the product.
They valued both versions equally regardless of effort invested.

biases.name: Loss aversion
biases.definition: Losses feel psychologically stronger than equivalent gains.

positive.text: He avoided investing entirely because potential losses felt more painful than possible gains.
She felt stronger distress losing five dollars than happiness from gaining the same amount.
Players quit games after small losses but continued after equivalent-sized wins.
Managers resisted budget cuts more intensely than they celebrated equivalent budget increases.
Students feared grade drops more than they valued potential grade improvements.

negative.text: She treated gains and losses symmetrically when making decisions.
A small loss felt no worse than an equivalent gain felt good.
Choices were guided by net outcomes, not fear of loss.

biases.name: Escalation of commitment
biases.definition: Continuing failing actions due to previous investments.

positive.text: They continued funding a doomed project because admitting failure would invalidate earlier investments.
She stayed in a failing relationship because of years already invested emotionally.
Managers doubled marketing spending to justify earlier unsuccessful campaigns.
Students stuck with wrong majors because switching felt like wasting previous coursework.
Teams extended bad contracts rather than admitting the initial decisions were mistakes.

negative.text: He stopped the project immediately after evidence showed it would fail.
Past investments did not influence the decision to withdraw.
They abandoned the plan despite prior effort and expense.

biases.name: Irrational escalation
biases.definition: Increasing commitment despite evidence of failure.

positive.text: She added more money to a scam even after clear warning signs appeared.
Companies expanded failing branches despite consistent financial losses.
Students repeated the same ineffective study methods despite poor exam results.
Gamblers chased losses by betting larger amounts after repeated failures.
Managers increased investment simply because walking away felt psychologically unbearable.

negative.text: She reduced commitment once results consistently worsened.
New evidence prompted disengagement rather than increased investment.
They accepted failure and redirected resources elsewhere.

biases.name: Sunk cost fallacy
biases.definition: Persisting because past costs cannot be recovered.

positive.text: He finished a terrible movie because he already paid for the ticket.
She stayed in a boring class because tuition had already been paid.
Travelers endured awful tours because they prepaid and refused to waste money.
They keep watching a boring movie because they already paid for the ticket.
Businesses kept operating unprofitable projects because significant money was already spent.

negative.text: He quit the course despite already paying the tuition.
Past expenses were ignored when deciding future actions.
She walked away once continuing no longer made sense.

categories.name: Motivated to keep autonomy and status in a group

biases.name: Status quo bias
biases.definition: Preference for maintaining current conditions even when better alternatives exist.

positive.text: People keep default phone settings despite knowing more efficient options exist.
Voters support existing policies simply because they are familiar.
Employees stay in inefficient workflows rather than adopting new systems.
Investors hold losing stocks to avoid changing their portfolios.
Users resist software updates despite promised performance improvements.

negative.text: They changed procedures quickly after identifying better alternatives.
She welcomed reform instead of preserving existing arrangements.
The group actively sought improvements over current practices.

biases.name: Social comparison bias
biases.definition: Judging oneself or decisions by comparison with others instead of absolutes.

positive.text: Student feels unsuccessful despite high grades because peers scored higher.
Employee undervalues promotion after comparing salary with coworkers.
Athlete feels inadequate after comparing performance to elite professionals.
Person buys luxury goods to match friends' lifestyles.
Researcher dismisses work because colleagues publish in higher journals.

negative.text: He evaluated success using personal goals rather than others' achievements.
Decisions were based on absolute standards, not peer comparisons.
She ignored social rankings when judging her performance.

biases.name: Decoy effect
biases.definition: Preference shifts toward option made attractive by an inferior comparison.

positive.text: Customers choose medium popcorn when overpriced large option is introduced.
Shoppers select mid-tier subscription after seeing an obviously worse alternative.
Diners order second-most-expensive wine due to extreme high-priced decoy.
Consumers prefer bundle once weaker bundle is added.
Buyers choose premium phone when low-value model is displayed.

negative.text: Preferences remained stable despite the introduction of inferior options.
She chose independently of how alternatives were framed.
The added option did not influence their original choice.

biases.name: Reverse psychology
biases.definition: Influencing behavior by suggesting the opposite of desired action.

positive.text: Parent tells child not to clean room, triggering immediate cleaning.
Coach doubts player's readiness, motivating improved performance.
Advertiser discourages purchase to increase perceived desirability.
Teacher warns assignment is too difficult, increasing student effort.
Friend suggests skipping event, making others more eager to attend.

negative.text: Clear instructions produced compliance without suggesting the opposite.
Direct requests worked better than indirect persuasion.
They responded positively to straightforward guidance.

biases.name: Reactance
biases.definition: Resistance arising when individuals feel their freedom of choice threatened.

positive.text: Teenagers want forbidden activities more after strict parental bans.
Employees resist mandatory policies even if beneficial.
Consumers dislike products heavily pushed by aggressive advertising.
People reject advice when phrased as commands.
Students oppose rules limiting expression.

negative.text: He accepted advice calmly without feeling his freedom threatened.
Guidelines were followed without resistance or defiance.
She welcomed recommendations rather than opposing them.

biases.name: System justification
biases.definition: Tendency to defend and legitimize existing social, economic, political systems.

positive.text: Workers justify unfair wages as necessary for economic stability.
Citizens defend unequal systems as natural or deserved.
Employees blame themselves instead of flawed organizational structures.
Marginalized groups accept stereotypes reinforcing existing hierarchies.
Voters rationalize corruption as unavoidable.

negative.text: They openly criticized the system instead of defending it.
Unfair structures were questioned rather than rationalized.
She supported change over preserving existing institutions.

categories.name: Favor simple-looking options & complete information

biases.name: Less-is-better effect
biases.definition: Smaller quantities judged more valuable when evaluated separately from larger ones.

positive.text: People prefer one perfect cookie over several imperfect ones.
Shoppers value a pristine gift set over larger damaged bundle.
Donors give more to single compelling story than statistics.
Recruiters favor concise resumes over longer detailed ones.
Buyers prefer fewer high-quality items.

negative.text: The larger set was judged more valuable even when evaluated separately.
He preferred greater quantity regardless of presentation context.
Value judgments increased consistently with size.

biases.name: Occam's razor
biases.definition: Preference for simpler explanations when multiple plausible explanations exist.

positive.text: Doctor favors common diagnosis over rare disease initially.
Engineer chooses straightforward design instead of complex alternative.
Analyst explains trend using fewer assumptions.
Student solves problem with simplest valid formula.
Investigator suspects simplest motive first.

negative.text: They favored a complex explanation supported by strong evidence.
Multiple interacting causes were accepted despite simplicity.
The simplest theory was rejected due to poor fit.

biases.name: Conjunction fallacy
biases.definition: Assuming specific combined events are more probable than single events.

positive.text: People believe detailed personality plus job description is more likely.
Jury assumes suspect committed multiple related crimes.
Readers judge complex story more realistic than simple explanation.
Investors expect startup to succeed in multiple ambitious markets.
Students think specific scenario is likelier than general one.

negative.text: She correctly judged single events as more probable than combined scenarios.
Probabilities were calculated using formal statistical reasoning.
They avoided intuitive but incorrect probability judgments.

biases.name: Delmore effect
biases.definition: Short tasks perceived longer when broken into multiple segments.

positive.text: Workers overestimate time for checklist with many small steps.
Students dread assignments divided into many subtasks.
Commuters feel trip longer when counting stops.
Gamers perceive missions longer when subdivided.
Runners feel workout longer with segmented intervals.

negative.text: Breaking the task into steps made it feel shorter.
Segmented tasks seemed easier and quicker to complete.
Perceived duration decreased after dividing the work.

biases.name: Law of Triviality
biases.definition: Disproportionate focus on trivial issues while ignoring important matters.

positive.text: Team debates logo color while ignoring system architecture.
Meeting fixates on formatting instead of strategy.
Committee argues about parking rather than budget allocation.
Developers discuss variable names, delaying core logic.
Board obsesses over minor expenses.

negative.text: The team focused discussion on critical issues over minor details.
Time was allocated according to importance, not simplicity.
Trivial matters were deliberately deprioritized.

biases.name: Belief bias
biases.definition: Judging arguments by believability rather than logical validity.

positive.text: People accept flawed reasoning because conclusion feels true.
Jurors trust arguments matching personal beliefs.
Students mark incorrect proofs as correct due to familiar outcomes.
Readers accept misinformation aligning with prior views.
Debaters favor agreeable conclusions.

negative.text: He rejected a believable argument because it was logically invalid.
Logical structure mattered more than conclusion plausibility.
She evaluated arguments strictly by formal reasoning.

biases.name: Bike-shedding effect
biases.definition: Over-discussing minor details while neglecting complex important decisions.

positive.text: Team spends hours on UI colors ignoring backend scalability.
Managers argue font choice instead of project risks.
Group debates lunch options during critical planning.
Engineers fixate on comments rather than algorithms.
Committee discusses naming instead of objectives.

negative.text: Meetings prioritized complex core decisions over cosmetic details.
Minor issues were skipped to address major design challenges.
The team avoided unnecessary discussion of trivial aspects.

biases.name: Rhyme as reason effect
biases.definition: Rhyming statements perceived as more truthful or persuasive.

positive.text: Slogans like no pain no gain feel convincing.
Rhyming advice is remembered and trusted more.
Jurors find rhymed arguments more credible.
Advertisements use rhymes to increase persuasion.
Proverbs rhyme to sound wise.

negative.text: A non-rhyming statement was trusted more due to strong evidence.
Rhyming slogans were dismissed as uninformative.
Persuasion depended on data, not poetic form.

biases.name: Information bias
biases.definition: Seeking additional information even when it does not improve decisions.

positive.text: Doctors order unnecessary tests despite clear diagnosis.
Managers request more reports delaying action.
Students over-research simple assignments.
Investors seek excessive data before obvious decisions.
Analysts collect metrics without impact.

negative.text: She stopped gathering data once it no longer improved decisions.
Only relevant information was collected before choosing.
Extra details were ignored to avoid analysis paralysis.

biases.name: Ambiguity bias
biases.definition: Avoiding options with unknown probabilities in favor of known risks.

positive.text: Investors prefer bonds over unfamiliar startups.
People choose known brands instead of new ones.
Gamblers avoid games with unclear odds.
Employees avoid innovative roles with uncertain outcomes.
Consumers reject unfamiliar technologies.

negative.text: He chose the option with unknown probabilities after careful evaluation.
Uncertain risks were accepted when potential benefits were higher.
They preferred flexibility over familiar but limited options.
